entries.meaning: The form of them that ordinary speech actually produces. A learner who listens for /ðɛm/ and hears nothing is hearing /əm/ perfectly well and not recognizing it.
examples: Just tell 'em the shipment is delayed.
I saw 'em leaving as I came in.
Round 'em up and get 'em on the truck.
Both of 'em said the same thing.
There's nothing left in the box — somebody took all of 'em.
Give 'em hell tomorrow.
entries.pronunciation note: also a syllabic /m̩/ after a consonant (tell 'em [ˈtɛl m̩]). It is never stressed and has no strong form; if the word carries stress it is them /ðɛm/.
entries.русский: их, им — редуцированное them в живой речи; на письме разг.
entries.register: neutral in speech, informal in writing — normal in dialogue, transcription, and advertising copy, out of place in a formal document
entries.type: personal pronoun, reduced (clitic)
entries.person / number: third person plural, and also singular where it is the reduced object form of singular they. Invariant for gender.
entries.refers to: exactly what them refers to — any plural antecedent, people or things, and a single person of unknown, unspecified, or nonbinary gender. It carries no dialect marking of its own: 'em in I saw 'em is what educated General American speakers produce in ordinary conversation, not a regional feature.
entries.agreement: none of its own — an object controls no verb.
entries.pattern: [verb] 'em · [verb] 'em [direct object] · [preposition] 'em · all/both/some of 'em · fixed phrases: give 'em hell, let 'em have it, sock it to 'em, round 'em up
entries.contrast: Against them: same word in function, different register in writing only — you may always write them where you hear 'em, and in edited prose you generally should, outside quoted speech. The apostrophe is standard and points backward at the missing sound. And the etymology is the real surprise — 'em is not a clipping of them. It descends from Middle English hem (Old English heom), the native third-person plural object pronoun, which the Norse-borrowed them displaced in the written language while the old form survived unstressed in the mouth. So them and 'em are two different words that ended up sharing one job.
entries.see also: them, they, him, themselves

entries.meaning: Points at a specific male person already identified, or one the listener can identify from context. It is subject-only: it can head a sentence, follow an auxiliary in a question, or sit in a coordinated subject, but it can never follow a verb or a preposition.
examples: He left the office before anyone could stop him.
Did he say when the shipment would arrive?
My brother and he were roommates for two years in Chicago.
He hasn't answered a single email since Thursday.
She types faster than he does, but he catches more mistakes.
Neither the landlord nor he had a key to the back door.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /i/ — the /h/ drops whenever he is unstressed and not at the start of an utterance: is he /ˈɪzi/, did he /ˈdɪdi/, would he /ˈwʊdi/, has he /ˈhæzi/
entries.русский: он — о мужчине или о животном, чей пол известен; о предметах — it
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun
entries.person / number: third person singular, masculine
entries.refers to: a male human being, or an animal whose sex is known and matters (a family pet, a named racehorse). Not things — for objects, abstractions, plants, and animals whose sex is unknown or irrelevant, use it. Some religious writing capitalizes He for God. Generic he covering a person of unspecified gender (Every applicant must submit his fingerprints) was the traditional rule and is now outdated in American English; use singular they or recast in the plural.
entries.agreement: third-person singular verb forms — he is, he was, he has, he does, he goes, he doesn't. Never he are. The bare present without -s (he go, he don't) is systematic in African American English and in some Southern varieties, but it is not standard written English.
entries.pattern: He [verb] · He [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] he [verb]? · [name] and he [plural verb] · than he [auxiliary] · It was he who [verb] (formal)
entries.contrast: He is the subject form, him the object form. Test by putting the pronoun alone in the slot: He arrived / I saw him — whichever sounds right alone is right in a coordination too (Marcus and he arrived, I saw Marcus and him). Do not confuse he with the possessive his, which never stands as a subject. After than and as, both cases are current: faster than he [is] is the formal conjunction reading, faster than him the ordinary spoken one.
entries.see also: him, she, they, it, his, himself

entries.term: he or she, him or her, s/he, himself or herself
entries.meaning: The compromise American editing reached in the 1970s, when generic he stopped being acceptable and singular they had not yet been accepted back. It is grammatically unimpeachable and stylistically expensive, and it now marks a document as a generation old — which is where a learner meets it: leases, policies, bylaws, statutes, and older textbooks.
examples: Each applicant is responsible for making sure that he or she has submitted a complete file.
Notify the account holder in writing before he or she is charged an overdraft fee.
The plan shall pay the participant the amount due him or her within sixty days of the request.
If a passenger's bag is lost, s/he should file a claim at the counter before leaving the airport.
No employee may approve a reimbursement to himself or herself.
A juror may not discuss the case with anyone, including his or her spouse. (the determiner half, which belongs with the determiners)
The same sentence as an American editor would write it today: All applicants are responsible for submitting a complete file.
entries.pronunciation note: the or is a weak /ɚ/ in ordinary speech, and in him or her /ˌhɪm ɚ ˈhɚ/ both /h/s drop: [ˌhɪm ɚ ˈɚ]. S/he has no pronunciation of its own — a reader says he or she aloud; the slash exists only on the page, and so do the older he/she and (s)he.
entries.русский: он или она — книжн. формула для лица неизвестного пола; вытеснена единственным they
entries.case: he or she subject, him or her object, himself or herself reflexive
entries.register: formal and dated — the house solution of American statutes, contracts, employee handbooks, insurance policies, and academic prose from roughly 1970 to 2010
entries.type: coordinated pronoun pair, epicene — gender-inclusive by listing both
entries.person / number: third person singular, and grammatically singular in every slot, which is exactly what it was built to be.
entries.refers to: one unidentified person of unstated gender — the each applicant, every employee, a juror of institutional prose. Never a specific person already named, and never a group. Two things pushed it out. It names two genders, so it excludes anyone who is neither and cannot be used for a person who has stated they or a neopronoun; and it doubles the length of every pronoun slot, which collapses after two repetitions — Each applicant must sign his or her form and bring it with him or her when he or she reports.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — he or she is responsible, he or she has thirty days. That is the cleanest difference from singular they, which takes a plural verb even for one person (they are responsible). The possessive determiner his or her precedes a noun and belongs to the determiner dictionary; the standalone possessive is his or hers.
entries.pattern: he or she [singular verb] · [verb] him or her · [preposition] him or her · [verb] himself or herself · s/he (writing only) · he or she, as the case may be (legal drafting) · he or she who [verb]
entries.variants: he/she, (s)he, s/he, she or he, her or him, herself or himself, he or she, as the case may be; the possessive halves his or her, his/her, and his or hers
entries.contrast: Against singular they, which is shorter, standard in edited American English, accepted by the major style guides, covers people of every gender, and takes a plural verb. Against generic he, which is dated in the other direction. In practice American editors now reach past both pronouns for a third repair — make the noun plural (All applicants must sign their forms) or cut the pronoun (Each applicant must submit a complete file) — because those remove the problem instead of managing it. The halves are not interchangeable across cases: ✗Give the form to he or she needs the object pair, him or her. And the reflexive still has to match a subject in its own clause, exactly as plain himself does: No employee may approve a payment to himself or herself.
entries.see also: he, she, they, them, his or hers, his or her (determiner), himself, herself, themself

entries.meaning: The object counterpart of she — it takes the direct object, indirect object, and object-of-preposition slots. It is also what Americans actually say after be (That's her), where traditional grammar prescribes she.
examples: I called her twice from the airport and got voicemail both times.
The committee offered her the position on Friday afternoon.
This envelope is for her, not for me.
Nobody had told her that the meeting was moved.
Give the spare key to Dana and her before you leave.
That's her in the second row, next to the window.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ɚ/ — the /h/ drops when unstressed and non-initial: tell her /ˈtɛlɚ/, give her /ˈɡɪvɚ/, ask her /ˈæskɚ/, call her /ˈkɔlɚ/ (homophonous with caller)
entries.русский: её, ей — объектная форма she; притяжательное her (her car) сюда не входит
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun
entries.person / number: third person singular, feminine
entries.refers to: a female human being, or an animal whose sex is known. The same word her is also the possessive determiner (her car) — that use belongs to the determiner dictionary and is not covered here. This entry is only the object pronoun: I called her.
entries.agreement: none of its own — an object controls no verb. When her follows be as a complement, the verb agrees with the subject, not with her: That's her, It was her who called (informal) / It was she who called (formal).
entries.pattern: [verb] her · [verb] her [direct object] · [preposition] her · [name] and her · That's her · than her
entries.contrast: Three words look alike and do different jobs. her = object pronoun (I saw her) or possessive determiner (her keys); hers = standalone possessive (The keys are hers); her's = not a word in any variety of English, ever. The test for object vs determiner is what follows: a noun after it makes it a determiner (her office), nothing after it makes it the object pronoun (I called her). Against she: she is the subject (She called), her the object (I called her).
entries.see also: she, him, them, hers, her (determiner), herself

entries.meaning: The object counterpart of he. It fills every non-subject slot, and in ordinary American speech it also fills the complement slot after be, where traditional grammar wants he.
examples: Tell him I'll be about ten minutes late.
We haven't seen him since the reunion in June.
The letter was addressed to him, but it came to my box.
Is that him in the blue jacket, or am I thinking of his brother?
She gave Marcus and him exactly the same instructions.
I've worked with him longer than anyone else on this floor.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ɪm/, sometimes /əm/ — tell him /ˈtɛlɪm/, get him /ˈɡɛɾɪm/, ask him /ˈæskɪm/. The /h/ survives only under stress or after a pause.
entries.русский: его, ему — объектная форма he
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun
entries.person / number: third person singular, masculine
entries.refers to: a male human being, or an animal whose sex is known and matters. Not things. Generic him for a person of unspecified gender (Ask each student to bring his own laptop) is outdated in American English — use singular them.
entries.agreement: none of its own — an object controls no verb. After be, the verb agrees with the subject: That's him, It was him (standard American) / It was he (formal, now stilted).
entries.pattern: [verb] him · [verb] him [direct object] · [preposition] him · [name] and him · That's him · than him
entries.contrast: He is the subject, him the object: He called me / I called him. Inside a coordination, delete the other name and the right form becomes obvious — The prize went to Marcus and him passes because The prize went to him passes, while ✗The prize went to Marcus and he fails the same test. Against his: his is possessive and never fills an object slot on its own (I called his is impossible). Against himself: use the reflexive only when the object is the same person as the subject of the same clause — He blamed himself vs. Marco said the manager would call him (different clauses, so the plain object form).
entries.see also: he, her, them, his, himself

entries.meaning: The speaker's own subject form. It heads a clause, inverts with an auxiliary in questions, and joins coordinated subjects — where politeness, not grammar, puts it last: My brother and I, not I and my brother.
examples: I disagree with the report's central conclusion.
My sister and I drove up to Vermont on Saturday morning.
Am I on the list, or did the registration never go through?
She has been at the firm longer than I have.
I have rewritten the opening paragraph three times and it still isn't right.
Neither the auditors nor I could find the missing invoice.
She and I went over the numbers twice before the meeting.
entries.pronunciation note: no true weak form — the vowel keeps its quality even unstressed, though the offglide shortens toward [ɑ] in fast speech (I dunno [ɑ dəˈnoʊ]) and across much of the South (I [aː]). The reductions happen in the contractions instead: I'm /aɪm/, I'll /aɪl/, I've /aɪv/, I'd /aɪd/.
entries.русский: я — только говорящий; в отличие от русского, опустить нельзя и пишется с заглавной
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun
entries.person / number: first person singular. Invariant for gender.
entries.refers to: the speaker or writer, and nobody else. In quoted or reported speech it shifts to whoever is doing the speaking, which is why "I'll pay," she said becomes She said she would pay.
entries.agreement: I is the only pronoun in English that takes am. Otherwise: I was, I have, I do, I go — the bare present, no -s. In the counterfactual subjunctive the form is were: If I were you.
entries.pattern: I [verb] · I [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] I [verb]? · [name] and I [plural verb] · than I [auxiliary] · It is I (formal, archaic-sounding)
entries.contrast: I is subject-only; me takes every other slot. The trap runs in both directions. The hypercorrection puts I into an object slot, and it is not confined to prepositions: ✗between you and I and ✗for my wife and I are objects of a preposition, but ✗They invited my wife and I and ✗She thanked Marcus and I are plain direct objects, and they are wrong for the same reason. This over-correction is now more common in educated American speech than the error it was invented to avoid. In the other direction, ✗Me and my friend are studying is nonstandard as a subject. The fix for both is the same: delete the other person. Send the invoice to Karen and → Send the invoice to me. They invited my wife and → They invited me. and my friend are studying → I am studying. Orthographically, I is the only English word capitalized wherever it appears.
entries.see also: me, we, mine, my (determiner), myself, you

entries.meaning: What a listener actually receives in place of him, her, and his. A learner who cannot find the pronoun in Did you tell him? is not missing it — there is no /h/ there to hear.
examples: Tell 'im I'll call back after five.
I gave 'er the keys and she drove off before I could explain the gate code.
Get 'im out of the sun and bring 'im some water.
What's 'is name — the guy who used to run the Denver office?
Let 'er rip. (a fixed phrase, where the referent is a machine, not a woman)
Somebody call 'im and find out whether the truck ever left the yard.
Ask 'er whether she wants the last of the coffee.
entries.pronunciation note: 'er is /ɚ/ (ur) and 'is is /ɪz/ (iz). All three are weak forms and nothing else — they are never stressed, and under stress the words are him /hɪm/, her /hɚ/, his /hɪz/. Linking and flapping across the boundary are normal: get 'im /ˈɡɛɾɪm/, tell 'er /ˈtɛlɚ/, what's 'is name → whatsisname /ˈwʌtsɪzˌneɪm/.
entries.русский: его, её, его (притяж.) — слабые формы him/her/his с выпадением /h/; разг. написание
entries.register: neutral in speech, informal in writing — dialogue, song lyrics, transcription, and advertising copy
entries.type: personal pronoun, reduced (weak forms)
entries.person / number: third person singular — 'im masculine object, 'er feminine object, 'is masculine possessive.
entries.refers to: exactly what him, her, and his refer to. The h-dropping is not a dialect feature. In American English the /h/ of an unstressed, non-initial pronoun deletes for every speaker in every region: I told him is [aɪ ˈtoʊldɪm], Ask her is [ˈæskɚ], That's his car is [ˈðæts ɪz ˈkɑr]. It is the ordinary output of General American at conversational speed, and it is not the British h-dropping of 'ouse and 'ammer, which deletes /h/ from full lexical words and is socially marked in England. Only the apostrophe spelling is informal; the sound is universal.
entries.agreement: none of their own — 'im and 'er are objects, and an object controls no verb; 'is is a possessive.
entries.pattern: [verb] 'im · [preposition] 'er · fixed phrases: tell 'im, get 'im, let 'er rip, give 'er hell, whatsisname, whatshername · 'is [noun] (the determiner use)
entries.variants: written without the apostrophe as im, er, is in some novelists' eye dialect; 'er also spells the reduced possessive determiner her ('er car)
entries.contrast: Against 'em: the same reduction one cell over in the paradigm, with one difference — 'em is a separate word historically, the descendant of Old English heom, while 'im, 'er, and 'is are simply him, her, and his minus the /h/. Against the page: spelling these forms in one character's mouth while writing him and her in the narrator's tells a reader that the character talks differently, when the narrator would reduce them too — that is the eye-dialect trap, and it is why editors cut these spellings from everything but deliberate dialogue. And the determiner line runs straight through this entry: 'is before a noun is a determiner, not a pronoun — 'is car is the reduced possessive determiner his, dictionaried with the determiners; only the standalone use (That one's 'is) is the pronoun his.
entries.see also: him, her, 'em, ya, he, his, his (determiner), himself

entries.meaning: It does more distinct jobs than any other pronoun in English, and only the first of them involves referring to anything.
examples: The printer jammed again this morning, and it took an hour to clear.
It has been raining since Tuesday and the field is unplayable.
It is unfortunate that the deadline fell on a holiday.
I find it strange that nobody from the office has called.
It was in Miami, not Atlanta, that they signed the agreement.
Don't overthink the presentation — just wing it.
Who is it? I wasn't expecting anyone.
The committee published its findings, and it stands by them.

senses.head: Referential
body: Stands for a thing, animal, or abstraction already named. The package arrived. It was damaged.

senses.head: Clausal / situational
body: Points back at an entire clause or an unnamed state of affairs. She quit without notice, and it put the whole project three weeks behind.

senses.head: Dummy subject
body: Weather, time, date, distance, temperature, and ambient conditions, where there is no subject to be had. It is snowing. It is almost midnight. It is three miles to the trailhead.

senses.head: Anticipatory subject
body: Holds the subject slot while the real subject, a clause, waits at the end. It is obvious that she was right (= That she was right is obvious).

senses.head: Anticipatory object
body: The same trick in object position, after verbs like find, make, think, consider. I find it strange that nobody called.

senses.head: Cleft focus
body: Splits a sentence to put the spotlight on one element. It was Daniel who signed the lease.

senses.head: Empty idiomatic object
body: A fixed object with no referent at all: make it, cool it, wing it, beat it, knock it off, lord it over someone, rough it, hoof it.
examples: The printer jammed again this morning, and it took an hour to clear.
It has been raining since Tuesday and the field is unplayable.
It is unfortunate that the deadline fell on a holiday.
I find it strange that nobody from the office has called.
It was in Miami, not Atlanta, that they signed the agreement.
Don't overthink the presentation — just wing it.
Who is it? I wasn't expecting anyone.
The committee published its findings, and it stands by them.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ət/; frequently ends in an unreleased or glottal [ɪʔ] before a pause (Forget it [fɚˈɡɛɾ ɪʔ]). Flapping across the boundary is normal: get it /ˈɡɛɾɪt/, put it /ˈpʊɾɪt/. The contraction it's is /ɪts/.
entries.русский: он, она, оно — о неодушевлённом и о животных; также формальное подлежащее без перевода
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun; also dummy (expletive) pronoun
entries.person / number: third person singular, neuter. Identical in both cases; no plural of its own — the plural is they/them.
entries.refers to: things, places, abstractions, substances, and animals whose sex is unknown or irrelevant; also a whole preceding clause or situation (The vendor missed three deadlines, and it cost us the contract). It cannot refer to a specific human being except in identification questions before the person is known (Who is it? — Someone's at the door) — and except where a person has chosen it/its as their own pronoun, which is a separate entry: it (as a chosen personal pronoun). Using it for a baby was once ordinary and now reads as cold; use he, she, or they. Traditional English called ships, boats, cars, and countries she; American style has largely moved to it, and Lloyd's List switched its own house style to it in 2002. In its dummy uses it refers to nothing at all — it simply fills the subject slot that English syntax insists on.
entries.agreement: third-person singular verb forms — it is, it was, it has, it does, it seems. This holds even in the dummy uses, and even when what follows is plural: It is the deadlines that worry me, though It's the deadlines is what people say. A collective noun takes it in American English (The committee released its findings) where British English often takes they.
entries.pattern: It [verb] · [verb] it · [preposition] it · It is [adjective] that [clause] · It was [focused element] that/who [clause] · [verb] it [adjective] that [clause] · It's [weather / time / distance]
entries.contrast: it (possessive-free pronoun) vs. its (possessive determiner, no apostrophe, the dog and its bone) vs. it's (contraction of it is or it has). The test never fails: if you can expand the word to it is or it has, write it's; otherwise write its. Against dummy there: both fill an empty subject slot, but there introduces the existence of something and hands agreement to the noun that follows (There are two options), while it keeps singular agreement always (It is two miles). Against they: a plural antecedent takes they, and in American English a collective noun takes it.
entries.see also: they, them, it (as a chosen personal pronoun), its (determiner), itself, this, that

entries.meaning: The speaker's object form, and the default first-person form everywhere except the subject slot — including as a one-word answer, after be, and as a fronted topic.
examples: The manager called me into her office before I'd even taken my coat off.
Give the extra ticket to Priya and me.
"Who wants the last slice?" — "Me."
Somebody knocked. "It's me," she said through the door.
Between you and me, that deal was dead a month ago.
Nobody warned me about the construction on Route 9.
Me, I'd have waited another week before signing anything.
entries.pronunciation note: no schwa weak form — unstressed me simply shortens (Tell me /ˈtɛl mi/, gimme /ˈɡɪmi/). The vowel stays /i/ in every position.
entries.русский: меня, мне, мной — объектная форма I
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun
entries.person / number: first person singular. Invariant for gender.
entries.refers to: the speaker or writer, and nobody else — the same referent as I, in a different grammatical slot.
entries.agreement: none of its own — an object controls no verb. When me follows be, the verb agrees with the subject: It's me, That was me. If a relative clause follows, the two registers split cleanly: It's me who's responsible (normal American) vs. It is I who am responsible (formal, and note the verb goes to am).
entries.pattern: [verb] me · [verb] me [direct object] · [preposition] me · [name] and me · It's me · than me · Me — (standalone answer) · Me, [clause] (topic)
entries.contrast: I is subject-only, me takes everything else. The two errors are mirror images. ✗Between you and I / ✗Send it to Karen and I / ✗They invited my wife and I — every one of those slots is an object slot (the first two after a preposition, the third a direct object), so the I is pure hypercorrection. ✗Me and him went to the concert — a subject slot takes the subject form. The deletion test settles both — remove the other person and read the sentence aloud. He gave it to Bob and → He gave it to me ✓, He gave it to I ✗. They invited my wife and → They invited me ✓, They invited I ✗. I went to the concert ✓, Me went to the concert ✗. Against myself: ✗Please contact Sara or myself — a reflexive needs a matching subject in the same clause, and myself is not a more polite me. One thing to unlearn: It's me is standard English, not an error. It is I is grammatically defensible and sounds stilted outside set phrases.
entries.see also: I, us, him, her, mine, myself

entries.meaning: The feminine third-person subject form. It heads a clause, inverts in questions, and joins coordinated subjects.
examples: She runs the entire East Coast operation out of a two-room office.
When did she get back from Denver?
She and her husband bought the building in 2019.
She hasn't returned any of my calls this week.
My mother reads faster than she does, but retains less.
"May I speak with Dr. Alvarez?" — "This is she."
entries.pronunciation note: no schwa weak form and no /h/ to drop — unstressed she just shortens (Did she /ˈdɪd ʃi/, often [ˈdɪtʃi] with assimilation). Contractions: she's /ʃiz/, she'll /ʃil/, she'd /ʃid/.
entries.русский: она — о женщине или о животном, чей пол известен; о предметах — it
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun
entries.person / number: third person singular, feminine
entries.refers to: a female human being, or an animal whose sex is known and matters. Not things, with one shrinking exception: ships, boats, cars, engines, and countries were traditionally she in English, and that convention now sounds dated in American prose — most style guides and most speakers use it. Hurricanes carried only female names until 1979 and alternating names since; either way a storm is it.
entries.agreement: third-person singular verb forms — she is, she was, she has, she does, she goes. Never she are.
entries.pattern: She [verb] · She [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] she [verb]? · [name] and she [plural verb] · than she [auxiliary] · This is she (telephone formula)
entries.contrast: She is the subject form, her the object form: She called me / I called her. In a coordination, test each half alone — Dana and she were hired the same week passes because She was hired passes. Do not confuse the subject she with the possessive determiner her or the standalone possessive hers. The one place she survives against the tide is the telephone formula This is she — a fossil of the old rule requiring the subject case after be, and the only context where most Americans still produce it.
entries.see also: her, he, they, it, hers, herself, this is he / this is she

entries.meaning: The only way English has of saying how many people a we, a you, or a they covers. It is a phrase rather than a word, but it fills a pronoun's slot, takes a pronoun's agreement, and does a job no single pronoun in the language does.
examples: The two of us signed the lease in March and moved in three weeks later.
The manager called the three of us into her office before we'd taken our coats off.
This stays between the two of us — don't bring it up at the meeting.
The four of them have been working the night shift since the plant reopened.
Can the two of you be at the airport by six, or should I go on ahead?
It's just the two of us for dinner tonight, so don't set the long table.
The both of us were out sick that week, which is why nobody answered the phone. (informal; both of us is the unmarked form)
entries.pronunciation note: one stress, on the numeral, and everything around it reduces — the is /ðə/, of falls to /ə/ or disappears, and the whole phrase runs together as [ðə ˈtuəvəs]. The both of us is /ðə ˈboʊθ əv ʌs/ (thuh-BOHTH-uv-uss) and the three of them /ðə ˈθri əv ðəm/ (thuh-THREE-uv-thum).
entries.русский: мы вдвоём, мы двое — точное указание числа группы: the three of you «вы втроём»
entries.case: subject and object alike; the phrase takes whatever slot it stands in, and the pronoun inside it is always the object form — of us, of you, of them, never ✗of we or ✗of they
entries.register: neutral, and usable in any register including a contract
entries.type: pronoun phrase (partitive) — the + a numeral or both + of + a personal pronoun
entries.person / number: first, second, or third person, and always plural in reference — the two of us, the three of you, the four of them. The numeral is doing arithmetic: it names the size of the group exactly, which is the one thing a bare personal pronoun cannot do.
entries.refers to: a specific group already identified, counted out in full. The two of us is the speaker plus one named or understood other; the three of them is a group of exactly three. It never introduces a group — the people have to be recoverable from context. People are the ordinary referent; the two of them can point at things (I bought two lamps and returned the two of them), but there it reads as clumsy beside plain both.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms, and the verb agrees with the numeral rather than with the pronoun inside: The two of us are driving up, The three of them were waiting at the gate, The both of us were out sick. Never ✗The two of us is. The reflexive matches too — the two of us blamed ourselves, the three of you should help yourselves.
entries.pattern: the [numeral] of us/you/them [plural verb] · [verb] the [numeral] of us/you/them · [preposition] the [numeral] of us/you/them · just the two of us · between the two of us · the both of us
entries.variants: the three of us, the four of them, the two of you, and on up through the numerals; the both of us, with both in the numeral slot, is the one member of the family that carries a register marking — it is informal, commonest in Southern and Irish-influenced American speech, and some editors cut the the; plain both of us, all three of us, and the two of us are unmarked everywhere
entries.contrast: Against bare we, you, and them, which leave the number open. That is not a small difference: the we entry names this phrase as the ordinary repair for the inclusive/exclusive ambiguity English has no grammar for — We're going to lunch is either an invitation or a dismissal, while The two of us are going to lunch is neither, because it has already said who. Against you two: same count, same people, different frame — you two is the appositive (pronoun + numeral), the two of you the partitive (the + numeral + of + pronoun). Both are standard; the partitive is a shade more formal on the page, and the appositive is the natural vocative (You two, over here beats The two of you, over here). Against both of us and all of us, which are the same construction with a quantifier instead of a numeral and are dictionaried with the quantifying pronouns. And the case rule inside the phrase is absolute: of is a preposition, so what follows it is an object form, whatever the phrase as a whole is doing in the sentence — The two of us signed has a subject-slot phrase built on the object pronoun us, and that is correct.
entries.see also: we, us, you two, you all, them, both, one, ourselves

entries.meaning: The object form of they, for plural referents and for singular they alike. It is also the form that survives in the reduced clitic 'em, which is what you will actually hear in nearly every casual sentence.
examples: I mailed them the signed contract on Tuesday.
We ran into them at the farmers' market on Saturday.
Ask them to call me back after four.
None of them fit, so I returned the whole box.
That's them pulling into the driveway now.
Somebody left an umbrella in the lobby — I'll hold it for them.
Just tell 'em the shipment is delayed.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ðəm/, reducing further to /əm/ and to a syllabic /m̩/ — get them /ˈɡɛɾəm/, tell them /ˈtɛləm/, give them /ˈɡɪvəm/. Written informally as 'em (entry), which is not a lazy spelling of them but the direct descendant of Middle English hem (Old English heom) — the native object pronoun that the Norse-borrowed them replaced on the page while it survived unstressed in the mouth.
entries.русский: их, им — объектная форма they; также об одном лице неизвестного или небинарного пола
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun
entries.person / number: third person; plural, and also singular when it is the object form of singular they. Invariant for gender.
entries.refers to: any plural antecedent — people, animals, things, abstractions, mixed groups. Also a single person of unknown, unspecified, or nonbinary gender (Somebody left their umbrella; put it aside for them). Also unspecified authorities or institutions in the generic sense (I called the city and they put me on hold; I never got them back on the line).
entries.agreement: none of its own — an object controls no verb. After be, the verb agrees with the subject: It was them, That's them now. In the quantifier patterns the verb agrees with the quantifier, not with them: Both of them are here, Each of them is here, and none of them takes either a singular or a plural verb — None of them fits (not one does) and None of them fit (no members do) are both standard, the plural being the older and commoner choice. See none.
entries.pattern: [verb] them · [verb] them [direct object] · [preposition] them · all/both/some/none of them · [name] and them · That's them
entries.contrast: They is the subject, them the object: They called me / I called them. Do not confuse the pronoun them with the nonstandard demonstrative them (them apples, them boys, Them are the ones) — that use is nonstandard, widespread in rural, Southern, Appalachian, and working-class American speech and marked wrong in all edited writing, and the standard form is those: them (demonstrative pronoun), them (demonstrative determiner), those. Keep the use separate from the pronunciation: the reduced /əm/ of I saw 'em carries no dialect marking at all and is ordinary General American. Against their/there/they're: them is never a possessive; the possessive determiner is their and the standalone possessive is theirs, neither of which takes an apostrophe.
entries.see also: they, 'em, us, him, her, theirs, themselves, them (nonstandard demonstrative), those

entries.meaning: The plural third-person subject form, and the general-purpose third-person singular when gender is unknown or not to be specified.
examples: The contractors finished early, and they left the site spotless.
They have been renovating that building for almost two years.
Whoever ordered this should confirm that they still want it.
Alex texted to say they were running late.
They say the bridge will be closed all summer.
Are they still planning to open the second location?
Every applicant must sign the waiver before they can start.

senses.head: Plural referential
body: Points back at a plural noun phrase of any kind. The files were water-damaged, so they had to be rescanned.

senses.head: Singular epicene
body: One person of unknown or unspecified gender. If a customer complains, ask them to fill out a form.

senses.head: Singular specific
body: One named person whose pronouns are they. Alex said they would email the draft tonight.

senses.head: Generic / hearsay
body: Unidentified people in general. They say it never rains here in July.

senses.head: Institutional
body: An organization the speaker does not bother to name. They changed the parking rules again.
examples: The contractors finished early, and they left the site spotless.
They have been renovating that building for almost two years.
Whoever ordered this should confirm that they still want it.
Alex texted to say they were running late.
They say the bridge will be closed all summer.
Are they still planning to open the second location?
Every applicant must sign the waiver before they can start.

entries.pronunciation note: no schwa weak form; the diphthong shortens toward [ðe] when unstressed. The contractions matter more than the reduction: they're is /ðɛr/ — identical to there and their in General American, and the one contraction that changes the vowel outright — while they'll /ðeɪl/, they've /ðeɪv/, and they'd /ðeɪd/ keep the diphthong, shortening it to [ðe-] only when unstressed.
entries.русский: они — также об одном лице неизвестного или небинарного пола, но глагол всегда во мн. ч.
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun
entries.person / number: third person; plural, and also singular in the epicene use. Invariant for gender in every use.
entries.refers to: any plural antecedent, human or not (The reports arrived late; they were incomplete). Also a single person whose gender is unknown, unspecified, or nonbinary. Also unidentified people in general (They say the winter will be mild) and unnamed institutions (They raised the rates again).
entries.agreement: always plural verb forms, including in the singular use — they are, they were, they have, they do. ✗They is and ✗they was are nonstandard in every variety of edited English, and singular they does not change this: Alex said they were coming, never they was coming. The reflexive is themselves, or themself when the referent is explicitly one person.
entries.pattern: They [plural verb] · They [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] they [verb]? · They say that [clause] · [singular antecedent] … they [plural verb]
entries.contrast: They is the subject, them the object. The homophone set is the most-misspelled trio in English: their (possessive determiner — their car), there (place, or the dummy subject — there is), they're (contraction of they are). All three are /ðɛr/ in speech; only the spelling separates them. Against he or she: singular they is standard American English, including in edited prose, and it is attested continuously from the late 1300s — Chaucer, Shakespeare, Austen — so it is not a recent invention. Merriam-Webster had long recorded the generic singular and added the specific nonbinary sense in 2019. The major American style guides accept it, with different scope: the APA Publication Manual endorses it outright and requires it for a person who uses it; the MLA Handbook accepts it generally; the Chicago Manual of Style accepts it without reservation for a person whose pronoun it is, and for a generic antecedent in all but the most formal registers; the AP Stylebook accepts it for people who use it and, in limited cases, generically, while still preferring a recast where one is natural. He or she now reads as clunky, and generic he reads as dated. What a conservative editor may still flag is inconsistency, not they itself: pick one strategy per passage and keep it.
entries.see also: them, 'em, we, he, she, it, theirs, themselves, their (determiner)

entries.meaning: The object form of we, filling every non-subject slot. It also appears in the appositive pattern us + noun, and inside the fossilized imperative let's.
examples: The neighbors invited us to dinner on Sunday.
Give us five more minutes and we'll have an answer.
The rezoning affects all of us on this side of the street.
They handed us editors a deadline nobody could have met.
Nobody had told us that the road was closed at the county line.
Let's get out of here before the lot fills up.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /əs/, reducing to bare /s/ in the fixed contraction let's /lɛts/ (= let us). Flapping across the boundary is normal: got us /ˈɡɑɾəs/.
entries.русский: нас, нам, нами — объектная форма we; включён ли собеседник, грамматически не показано
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun
entries.person / number: first person plural. Invariant for gender.
entries.refers to: the speaker together with at least one other person. Whether the listener is included is not marked grammatically — English has no separate inclusive and exclusive forms, so He invited us leaves it to context whether you are in the group.
entries.agreement: none of its own — an object controls no verb. After be, the verb agrees with the subject: It was us, That's us in the back row.
entries.pattern: [verb] us · [verb] us [direct object] · [preposition] us · all/both/some/none of us · us [plural noun] (appositive) · Let's [verb] · than us
entries.contrast: We is the subject, us the object: We hired them / They hired us. The appositive pair is worth memorizing because both forms are correct in different slots: We editors work late (subject) but They gave us editors a deadline (object) — delete the noun and the case is obvious. ✗Us guys went to the game is nonstandard for the same reason. Let's is let us contracted, and the doubled ✗let's us go is dialectal. In British and Irish English us can informally mean me (Give us a minute); this is marginal in American speech and best avoided in writing.
entries.see also: we, me, them, ours, ourselves

entries.meaning: Beyond its ordinary plural sense, we carries five special uses. Four of them — the editorial, the authorial, the royal, and the nurse's we — are plural in grammar but singular in what they actually refer to; the fifth, the generic, is wider than any group the speaker could point at. All six take a plural verb, without exception: the royal we and the editorial we are we are, never we is.
examples: We signed the lease in March and moved in three weeks later.
Are we still meeting at eight, or has that shifted?
We still don't understand why the effect disappears at low temperatures.
We Midwesterners have a complicated relationship with February.
In this paper we argue that the reported gains were an artifact of the sampling.
We endorse the bond measure and urge a yes vote in November. (the paper's editorial, written by one person and signed by none)
We granted certiorari to resolve a conflict among the circuits. (a court speaking as itself)
"And how are we feeling this morning?" the nurse asked, reaching for the chart.
We have not yet decided whether to grant the petition.

senses.head: Ordinary plural
body: The speaker and at least one other. We signed the lease in March.

senses.head: Generic / universal
body: Humanity, or everyone in a shared situation. We still don't know what causes most migraines.

senses.head: Editorial
body: A publication or an institution speaking in its own voice, whoever typed the sentence: an unsigned newspaper editorial (We endorse the bond measure), a magazine's house style, a court speaking for itself in an opinion (We granted certiorari to resolve the conflict among the circuits). One person writes it; the institution says it, which is why the byline is absent and the verb is still plural.

senses.head: Authorial
body: A single author using the plural in academic, scientific, or technical prose. In this paper we argue that the effect is overstated. It is a convention of the genre rather than a claim about how many people did the work, and the mathematician's version of it — we now differentiate both sides — sweeps the reader in alongside the author. Several American style guides, the APA manual among them, now tell a sole author to write I.

senses.head: Royal (the majestic plural)
body: A monarch, and formerly a pope, speaking as the institution rather than as a person. We are not amused, the line traditionally attributed to Queen Victoria and probably never said by her. Archaic in American English outside historical writing, satire, and the joke about having a mouse in one's pocket.

senses.head: The nurse's we (the patronizing or paternal we)
body: A caregiver, teacher, or clinician using we for a you that is doing all the work. How are we feeling today? Are we ready to try a few steps? Warm and inclusive when the rapport is there, condescending when it isn't — many patients dislike it, and it is worth recognizing rather than adopting.
examples: We signed the lease in March and moved in three weeks later.
Are we still meeting at eight, or has that shifted?
We still don't understand why the effect disappears at low temperatures.
We Midwesterners have a complicated relationship with February.
In this paper we argue that the reported gains were an artifact of the sampling.
We endorse the bond measure and urge a yes vote in November. (the paper's editorial, written by one person and signed by none)
We granted certiorari to resolve a conflict among the circuits. (a court speaking as itself)
"And how are we feeling this morning?" the nurse asked, reaching for the chart.
We have not yet decided whether to grant the petition.

entries.pronunciation note: no schwa weak form; the vowel shortens when unstressed. The contractions do reduce: we're is often /wɚ/ in fast speech, which is why we're and were collide (We're going [wɚ ˈɡoʊɪn]); we'll /wil/ or /wɪl/, we've /wiv/, we'd /wid/.
entries.русский: мы — говорящий и другие; «мы с тобой» и «мы без тебя» не различаются
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun
entries.person / number: first person plural. Invariant for gender.
entries.refers to: the speaker plus at least one other. English does not grammatically distinguish inclusive we (speaker + listener) from exclusive we (speaker + others, not you), unlike Tagalog, Cherokee, or Mandarin's zánmen. We're going to lunch is genuinely ambiguous between an invitation and an announcement, and speakers disambiguate with a following phrase — we all, the two of us, you and I.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms — we are, we were, we have, we do, and the bare present with no -s (we go). This holds even in the singular-reference uses: the royal we and the editorial we still take we are, never we is.
entries.pattern: We [plural verb] · We [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] we [verb]? · We [plural noun] [verb] (appositive) · Let's [verb] · than we [auxiliary]
entries.contrast: We is the subject, us the object. The appositive test is the one to keep: We editors work late / They gave us editors a deadline — delete the noun and the case falls out. Against the possessives: our precedes a noun (our office), ours stands alone (The corner office is ours), and neither takes an apostrophe.
entries.see also: us, I, they, ours, ourselves, one

entries.meaning: The weak form of you, written down. A learner listening for /ju/ and hearing nothing has heard /jə/ perfectly well without recognizing it — and most often has not even heard that, because the sound has been swallowed into the /dʒ/ or /tʃ/ at the end of the previous word.
examples: See ya Monday — I'll leave the keys at the front desk.
I'll call ya as soon as the flight lands.
Ya never know what the market is going to do.
This one's for ya, and don't say I never gave you anything.
How ya doin'? I haven't seen you since the spring.
Did anybody tell ya the meeting moved to Thursday?
Ya got a minute, or should I come back later?
entries.pronunciation note: never stressed and with no strong form of its own — if the word carries stress it is you /ju/. After /t/ or /d/ it does not surface as a separate syllable at all but fuses with the word before it: did ya /ˈdɪdʒə/, don't ya /ˈdoʊntʃə/, got ya → gotcha /ˈɡɑtʃə/, what do ya → whaddaya /ˈwʌɾəjə/.
entries.русский: ты, вы — редуцированное you; разг. написание, не диалект
entries.register: neutral in speech, informal in writing — normal in dialogue, lyrics, advertising copy, and transcription, out of place in a formal document
entries.type: personal pronoun, reduced (weak form)
entries.person / number: second person, singular and plural, subject and object alike — it inherits every cell of you and, like you, marks neither number nor case.
entries.refers to: exactly what you refers to — the person or people being addressed, and, in the generic sense, anybody at all (Ya never know). It carries no dialect marking of its own: /jə/ is what educated General American speakers produce for unstressed you in ordinary conversation, and the spelling ya only writes that down. It is not Southern, not working-class, and not a plural.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms, even for one person, exactly as with you — ya are, ya were, ya have, ya do, never ✗ya is. Reducing the pronoun changes nothing about the conjugation.
entries.pattern: [verb] ya · [preposition] ya · Ya [plural verb] · [auxiliary] ya [verb]? · fixed phrases: See ya, Catch ya later, How ya doin'?, Ya know?, Gotcha
entries.contrast: Against you: the same word in its weak form, differing in writing only — you may always write you where you hear ya, and in edited prose you generally should, outside quoted speech. Against 'em: the same relationship, one person up the paradigm, except that 'em is a distinct word historically while ya is nothing but you at speed. Against y'all, youse, and you'uns: those are built forms — plural-only, and regionally or socially marked; ya is neither built nor plural nor marked. And it is never a possessive: the reduced possessive is yer/your /jɚ/ (Watch yer step), and the reduced you are is y'r or plain you're.
entries.see also: you, 'em, y'all, you all, yours, your (determiner), yourself, yourselves

entries.meaning: One word doing four jobs, which is why American English keeps inventing plural forms for it. You is the subject, the object, the singular, and the plural, and nothing in the form itself tells you which.
examples: You left your badge on the kitchen counter again.
Did you two ever hear back from the insurance company?
I'll email you the revised numbers before Friday.
You can't get a building permit in this county without an appointment.
This one is for you and this one is for your sister.
You go first — I'll hold the door.
If you were in charge, what would you change?

senses.head: Singular addressee
body: One person. You left your badge on the counter.

senses.head: Plural addressee
body: A group, unmarked. You all need to sign in at the front desk.

senses.head: Generic
body: Anyone, people in general. You can't get a permit without an appointment.

senses.head: Emphatic / vocative in imperatives
body: Normally the imperative has no subject, but you can be inserted for contrast or force. You go first. Don't you touch that.
examples: You left your badge on the kitchen counter again.
Did you two ever hear back from the insurance company?
I'll email you the revised numbers before Friday.
You can't get a building permit in this county without an appointment.
This one is for you and this one is for your sister.
You go first — I'll hold the door.
If you were in charge, what would you change?

entries.pronunciation note: weak /jə/ and /jʊ/ — and, more than any other pronoun, you fuses with the word before it: did you /ˈdɪdʒə/, don't you /ˈdoʊntʃə/, would you /ˈwʊdʒə/, what do you → whaddaya /ˈwʌɾəjə/, got you → gotcha /ˈɡɑtʃə/. Learners who cannot hear you are usually hearing it perfectly well as the /dʒ/ or /tʃ/ at the end of the previous word. The weak form is spelled ya in dialogue and casual writing (See ya, How ya doin'?, Thank ya) — that spelling records the ordinary reduction of standard you and marks no region and no dialect; it is informal on the page, not nonstandard in the mouth. It has its own entry: ya.
entries.русский: ты, вы — к одному и ко многим; различия ты/вы и ед./мн. ч. в английском нет
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: personal pronoun
entries.person / number: second person, singular and plural, subject and object — one form for all four. Only the reflexive distinguishes number: yourself (one person) vs. yourselves (more than one).
entries.refers to: the person or people being addressed. Also, in the generic sense, anybody at all (You never know what the market will do), where it is the informal counterpart of formal one.
entries.agreement: always plural verb forms, even for one person — you are, you were, you have, you do, never ✗you is. This is a historical fossil: you was originally the plural, and it drove out the singular thou in the seventeenth century, taking the plural verb with it. ✗You was was ordinary educated English in the eighteenth century and survives today as a systematic feature of Southern American English, African American English, and working-class varieties nationwide, alongside we was and they was; all of them are nonstandard in edited English. The counterfactual is if you were.
entries.pattern: You [plural verb] · [verb] you · [preposition] you · [auxiliary] you [verb]? · You [verb]! (emphatic imperative) · you [plural noun] (appositive: you people) · You never know (generic)
entries.contrast: The apostrophe pair is the trap: your is the possessive determiner (your keys), you're is the contraction of you are (you're late), and yours — no apostrophe, ever — is the standalone possessive (the blue one is yours). Expand it: if you are fits, write you're. Against one: generic you is normal American English in speech and ordinary writing (You have to file by April 15), while one is the formal register (One must file by April 15) — the error is drifting between them in a single passage. Against the plural workarounds below: none of y'all, you guys, youse, yinz belongs in formal writing; when the plural genuinely needs marking there, write all of you, you all, both of you, or name the group.
entries.see also: ya, yours, your (determiner), yourself, yourselves, y'all, you all, you guys, youse, you'uns, thou, one

entries.meaning: The plural you that a document can use. English lost its second-person plural when thou died out, and every regional replacement in the next section is marked in some way; you plus a numeral is the repair that costs nothing, and it has the bonus of saying exactly how many.
examples: Did you two ever hear back from the insurance company?
I'll meet you two at the gate about a half hour before boarding.
You two — over here, please. The rest can wait in the hall.
Have you both signed the acknowledgment at the bottom of page three?
This applies to you three as well, not just to the two who were in the room.
Help yourselves to the coffee; there's more than enough for you two.
Is that you two's car in the loading zone? (informal; in writing, the two of you)
entries.pronunciation note: weak /jəˈtu/ — yə-TOO; the stress falls on the numeral and the two words are said as one unit, exactly as in you guys. You both is /juˈboʊθ/ (yoo-BOHTH) and you three /juˈθri/ (yoo-THREE).
entries.русский: вы двое, вы оба — you с числительным; нейтрально, годится и для письма
entries.case: subject and object alike, like you itself
entries.register: neutral — with you all, one of the only two plural-you forms that survive editing unchanged; it is not regional, not informal, and not gendered
entries.type: personal pronoun (phrasal) — the appositive you + a numeral, the same frame as you guys, you people, and you editors
entries.person / number: second person plural, and exactly counted. You two is two people and you three is three, which is what separates this frame from every other plural you in the file: y'all, you guys, youse, you'uns, and you all all leave the number open.
entries.refers to: the people being addressed, counted. In the vocative it does a second job — singling a pair out of a larger room (You two, over here) — and in that use the count is doing the pointing. It is not a group label the way you guys is, and it carries none of the freight of you people.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms — you two are, you two were, you two have, you two do, never ✗you two is. Since the referent is more than one, the reflexive is yourselves, never ✗yourself: Help yourselves to the coffee.
entries.pattern: You two [plural verb] · [verb] you two · [preposition] you two · You two! (vocative) · you both · you three, you four · you two's [noun] (informal possessive)
entries.variants: you both, you three, you four, and on up; the partitive equivalents the two of you, the three of you and both of you; the possessive you two's (Is that you two's car?) is spoken rather than written, and edited prose recasts it as your or the two of you
entries.contrast: Same appositive frame as you guys and you people — you plus a nominal, taking the case of its slot, exactly like the us editors pattern under us. What makes it different is that it is unmarked: you guys is informal and under pressure for being gendered, you people lands as hostile, y'all and youse are regional, and you two is none of these. Against the partitive the two of you: same count and same people, both standard, and the choice is register and position — the partitive reads slightly more formally as a subject, the appositive is what a speaker actually says in the vocative. Against singular you: the number is the whole point, so You two need to sign says something You need to sign does not, and it is the cheapest way to disambiguate an American you without reaching for a regional form.
entries.see also: you, you all, you guys, you people, the two of us, y'all, us, yourselves

entries.meaning: The object form of thou, driven out of general English by you in the seventeenth century. It survived in Quaker plain speech into the twentieth century, in the King James Bible, in hymns and prayers, and in poetry reaching for an older register.
examples: I will not leave thee, nor forsake thee.
The Lord bless thee and keep thee.
How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.
Get thee to a nunnery.
The Lord make his face shine upon thee. (object of a preposition)
Thee is welcome to stay as long as thee likes, Friend. (Quaker usage)
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form in modern liturgical reading
entries.русский: тебя, тебе — устар., объектная форма thou; книжн., церк., поэт.
entries.register: archaic, liturgical, poetic
entries.type: personal pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: second person singular
entries.refers to: one person being addressed — historically an intimate, a subordinate, a child, or God. Never a group; the plural was ye and later you.
entries.agreement: none of its own as an object. In Quaker plain speech, where thee was extended to subject position, it took the third-person singular verb: Thee is right, Thee has forgotten — not the -est ending that goes with thou.
entries.pattern: [verb] thee · [preposition] thee · thee [third-person verb] (Quaker usage only)
entries.contrast: Thou is the subject, thee the object — exactly the I/me and he/him split: Thou art late / I saw thee. The possessives are thy before a consonant, thine before a vowel or standing alone (thy hand, thine eyes, the fault is thine). Do not use thee as a subject when imitating Shakespeare or the King James Bible; that pattern belongs specifically to nineteenth- and twentieth-century Quaker speech, not to Early Modern English.
entries.see also: thou, ye, you

entries.meaning: The old singular subject you, lost from general English around 1650 and preserved now only in scripture, hymns, prayer, poetry, and deliberate archaism. It survives in living speech in parts of northern England, not in the United States.
examples: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor.
Thou art the man.
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? Thou art more lovely and more temperate.
Where wilt thou go, and what wilt thou do there?
Thou hast forgotten who gave thee that ring.
entries.русский: ты — устар., фамильярное ед. ч. при вежливом you, как франц. tu; книжн., церк.
entries.register: archaic, liturgical, poetic
entries.type: personal pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: second person singular
entries.refers to: one person being addressed. In Early Modern English it was the familiar singular — used to intimates, children, servants, and God — while you was the plural and the polite singular, exactly like French tu and vous. Using thou to a social superior was a calculated insult; the verb to thou meant precisely that.
entries.agreement: takes its own verb ending, -est or -st: thou goest, thou hast, thou art, thou wilt, thou shalt, thou didst, thou canst. This ending exists nowhere else in the language and is the surest marker of the register.
entries.pattern: Thou [verb + -est] · Thou art [complement] · [auxiliary + -st] thou [verb]?
entries.contrast: Thou is the subject and thee the object, the same split as he/him. Its disappearance is why modern you takes plural agreement (you are) even for one person — you won, and it brought the plural verb with it. Standard American English has no trace of thou; the second-person singular/plural distinction it once carried is now rebuilt informally as y'all and you guys.
entries.see also: thee, ye, you

entries.meaning: The Appalachian and South Midland first-person plural, built from we ones on the same pattern as you'uns. It is the rarest of the built pronouns in this file and is now heard mainly from older speakers.
examples: We'uns have farmed this hollow for four generations.
Are you'uns driving up, or should we'uns come down to meet you?
He never had much use for us'uns.
We'uns were finished before the rain started.
That strip of bottomland belongs to us'uns, not to the county.
entries.pronunciation note: also written we-uns; the object form is us'uns /ˈʌsənz/ · USS-unz
entries.русский: мы — диал. (Аппалачи), в противопоставлении you'uns; вне литературной нормы
entries.case: subject we'uns, object us'uns — the one built form in this section that keeps a case distinction
entries.register: nonstandard, strongly regionally marked, receding
entries.type: personal pronoun, regional
entries.person / number: first person plural. From we ones, built exactly like you'uns from you ones, and carried by the same Scots-Irish settlement.
entries.refers to: the speaker together with the group the speaker belongs to — a family, a household, a hollow, a side — almost always in explicit or implied contrast with some other group, typically you'uns. That contrastive force is the whole point of the form, since standard we already covers the plural perfectly well.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms — we'uns are, we'uns were, we'uns have, we'uns do. Us'uns, being an object, controls no verb at all.
entries.pattern: We'uns [plural verb] · [verb] us'uns · [preposition] us'uns · we'uns and you'uns
entries.contrast: We'uns is the first-person mate of you'uns, and the pair is the reason this section is not entirely about the second person. The two are not parallel in what they accomplish: you'uns fills a real hole in the standard paradigm, since English has no plural you, while we'uns fills nothing and survives on contrast alone — which is why it is receding faster. Both are Appalachian and South Midland, both are nonstandard in writing, and we'uns in particular reads as an imitation of the region in anyone who did not grow up with it. Against us: us is the standard object form and takes every slot us'uns takes.
entries.see also: you'uns, we, us, y'all, we'uns (archaic and dialectal)

entries.meaning: The Southern and African American English second-person plural, and the most widely adopted of the American plural-you forms. Within those varieties it is unremarkable, fully standard speech; outside them it is informal but no longer marked as uneducated.
examples: Y'all coming to the cookout on Saturday?
I'll see y'all at the church at six.
This one's for y'all — don't open it till Christmas.
Is that y'all's truck blocking the driveway?
All y'all need to be on the bus by seven sharp.
entries.pronunciation note: one syllable; the two-syllable /jəˈɔl/ is you all, a different item
entries.русский: вы, вы все — южн. и афроам. англ.; часто «ты и твои», разг. вне Юга
entries.register: informal; standard within Southern American English and African American English, informal elsewhere
entries.type: personal pronoun, regional
entries.person / number: second person plural. Contracted from you all, and the apostrophe marks the missing letters of you — y'all, not ✗ya'll.
entries.refers to: the group being addressed. Often associative as well as plural: y'all can mean "you and the people who go with you" — Is y'all coming Sunday? said to one person can mean "you and your family." Whether y'all is ever truly singular is genuinely disputed; linguists document singular uses, most native speakers report only the plural and associative ones, and outsiders who use it as a singular mark themselves immediately.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms — y'all are, y'all were, y'all have.
entries.pattern: Y'all [plural verb] · [verb] y'all · [preposition] y'all · all y'all (intensified, unambiguously the whole group) · y'all's [noun] (possessive)
entries.contrast: Y'all is the Southern and African American English plural you; you guys is the national informal equivalent; youse is the northeastern urban one; you'uns and yinz are western Pennsylvanian. All four fill the gap left when thou died and you absorbed both numbers. Y'all is spreading well beyond the South, partly because it is the only one of the four that is not gendered and not regionally stigmatized outside its home range. Its possessive is y'all's; the plural-of-a-plural all y'all is standard within the dialect and is not redundant — it forces the reading "every one of you."
entries.see also: you, you all, you guys, youse, you'uns

entries.meaning: The archaic plural subject you. It survives in scripture, hymns, proclamations, and set phrases, and in the mock-antique register of tavern signs.
examples: Ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
Gather ye rosebuds while ye may.
O come, all ye faithful.
Hear ye, hear ye: this court is now in session.
Ye of little faith, why are ye so fearful?
entries.русский: вы — устар., мн. ч. подлежащего; книжн., библ., поэт.
entries.case: originally subject; later subject and object alike
entries.register: archaic, liturgical, poetic
entries.type: personal pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: second person plural (later also the polite singular)
entries.refers to: the group being addressed. In the oldest layer of the system ye was the plural subject and you the plural object (Ye shall know the truth / I say unto you); by the sixteenth century the two had blurred, and you eventually took over both.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms — ye are, ye have, ye shall — never the -est ending, which belongs to thou.
entries.pattern: Ye [plural verb] · Hear ye · [imperative] ye
entries.contrast: Ye is the plural of thou, so the full archaic set is thou/thee (one person) against ye/you (more than one). The Ye in Ye Olde Shoppe is a completely different word. It is not the pronoun at all — it is the definite article the, written with the Old English letter thorn (þ) that early printers, lacking the type, replaced with a y. It was always pronounced /ðə/, and the modern spelling-pronunciation /ji ˈoʊldi/ is a joke the sign painters started.
entries.see also: thou, thee, you

entries.meaning: Linguists working in Baltimore middle schools in the mid-2000s noticed students using yo where standard English needs he or she, and described it in American Speech in 2007. It remains local, adolescent, and spoken, and it is the rarest thing in this whole file: a gender-neutral third-person singular that appeared in ordinary American speech with no campaign behind it.
examples: Yo was tuckin' in his shirt. (the recorded pattern — the pronoun is neutral, the possessive that follows it is not)
Yo threw a thumbtack at me and then acted like nothing happened.
Ask yo whether the late bus already came.
Yo is in my math class, second period.
I gave the hall pass back to yo after lunch.
Yo wasn't even in the building when it happened.
Look at yo — yo got new shoes on.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — it is one short syllable and normally carries at least secondary stress. It is a perfect homophone of two other words spelled the same way: the nationwide interjection yo (Yo! Over here) and the vernacular possessive determiner yo (yo mama), which is your with the /r/ gone.
entries.русский: он, она — диал. (Балтимор), о присутствующем лице без указания пола; вне нормы
entries.register: nonstandard and tightly regional — Baltimore-area vernacular, chiefly adolescent and chiefly within African American English. It is a spoken form only: it does not appear in edited writing, it is not part of adult standard speech in any region, and outside Baltimore most Americans have never heard it used this way.
entries.type: personal pronoun, regional and nonstandard — a spontaneously arisen third-person singular
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral, invariant for case.
entries.refers to: one person, ordinarily one who is present or in sight — the recorded uses are overwhelmingly about somebody in the room, across the hall, or down the block, and often about somebody whose gender the speaker knows perfectly well and simply does not mark. Never a group, never a thing, and never a hypothetical or generic person.
entries.agreement: third-person singular verb forms — yo is, yo was, yo has, yo does. That is the sharpest difference from singular they, which keeps a plural verb even for one person (they are).
entries.pattern: Yo [singular verb] · Yo [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] yo [verb]? · [verb] yo · [preposition] yo
entries.variants: none recorded; the study that documented it found no possessive of its own — speakers filled that slot with the ordinary his, her, or their (Yo was tuckin' in his shirt), which is one reason it is described as a partial paradigm rather than a full set
entries.contrast: Three different words share the spelling, and only one of them is this pronoun. The interjection yo — Yo, hold the door — is nationwide, informal, and fills no noun-phrase slot at all. And yo meaning your precedes a noun, which makes it a determiner, not a pronoun: yo car belongs with the possessive determiners. Against singular they: the same job, a different verb (yo is against they are), and an incomparably smaller reach — they is standard nationwide and centuries old, yo is a local vernacular form used by a few thousand speakers in one city. Against the neopronouns: those are proposals, adopted deliberately by people who state them, and yo is the opposite case — nobody coined it, nobody advocates for it, and no speaker announces it. That is exactly why it drew attention. Dennis Baron's survey of the record turns up more than two hundred invented gender-neutral pronouns since the 1780s and not one general success; yo arrived on its own. It is still a form to recognize rather than to produce: it belongs in no document, and an outsider using it marks themselves the way yinz does outside Pittsburgh.
entries.see also: they, he, she, y'all, neopronouns and chosen pronoun sets, your (determiner)

entries.meaning: The plain, unmarked American plural you, and, beside the counted you two, the member of the family that survives editing. It is also the source of y'all, though speakers who use both keep them distinct.
examples: You all need to be at the gate by six.
Thank you all for coming out on such short notice.
I'd like you all to look at the second page.
This policy applies to all of you, without exception.
Are you all riding together, or should I hold two spaces?
entries.pronunciation note: two syllables, stress on all
entries.русский: вы все — мн. ч. от you, подчёркнуто без исключений; допустимо на письме
entries.register: informal to neutral; the least marked of the plural-you forms, and one of only two — with the counted you two — usable in careful writing
entries.type: personal pronoun (phrasal)
entries.person / number: second person plural
entries.refers to: everyone in the group being addressed, with no exceptions — the all is doing real work, which is why the phrase reads as inclusive rather than merely plural.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms — you all are, you all were.
entries.pattern: You all [plural verb] · [verb] you all · all of you (the inverted variant, more formal) · Thank you all
entries.contrast: You all is the uncontracted source of y'all, but the two are not interchangeable in register: you all is unmarked nationwide, while y'all is regionally and socially marked. The near-synonym all of you is the most formal of the set and is the one to use when a document genuinely has to address a group (This applies to all of you). None of y'all, you guys, youse, or yinz would do there.
entries.see also: you, y'all, you guys, you two, the two of us

entries.meaning: The default informal American plural you, current in every region and almost every register short of writing. Grammatically it has fused: it takes a possessive as a unit, and speakers apply it without reference to the gender of anyone in the group.
examples: Are you guys ready to order, or do you need another minute?
I'll meet you guys downstairs in ten.
Did anyone bring you guys the updated schedule?
Is this you guys' car in the loading zone?
You guys have been incredibly patient with all of this.
entries.русский: вы, ребята — разг., о группе любого пола; не для письменной речи
entries.register: informal, nationwide; not for writing
entries.type: personal pronoun (phrasal)
entries.person / number: second person plural
entries.refers to: the group being addressed, of any gender composition — you guys is routinely used for all-female and mixed groups across the United States, which is why it is not simply the plural of guy. That said, a growing number of speakers and institutions avoid it precisely because the singular is gendered, and substitute you all, folks, everyone, or team.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms — you guys are, you guys were.
entries.pattern: You guys [plural verb] · [verb] you guys · [preposition] you guys · you guys' [noun] (possessive)
entries.contrast: You guys is the national informal plural you; y'all is the Southern one, youse the northeastern urban one, you'uns/yinz the Pittsburgh one. Of these, you guys has the widest geographic reach and the shakiest future — it is the only one under active pressure for being gendered, and y'all and you all are the usual replacements. Its possessive you guys' is written with the apostrophe after the s, which is one sign of how far the phrase has traveled from being a real noun phrase.
entries.see also: you, you all, y'all, youse

entries.meaning: The one American plural you whose difficulty is not its grammar. Recognize it, understand why it lands the way it does, and reach for a different plural.
examples: "You people don't understand how this neighborhood works," he said, and the room went quiet.
Every time a candidate says you people in a speech, the next day's coverage is about the phrase instead of the policy.
You people in the back — can you hear me all right?
She caught herself halfway through: "You people — sorry, all of you — need to sign in at the desk."
He insisted he meant nothing by you people, which is the whole difficulty: a speaker does not get to decide alone how it lands.
The newsroom style guide tells reporters to quote you people exactly when a source says it and never to use it in their own voice.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /jəˈpipəl/ — yə-PEE-pul; the stress falls on people, and the two words are said as one unit
entries.русский: вы, эти ваши — разг., звучит враждебно: обращение к людям как к категории
entries.register: informal, nationwide, and pragmatically loaded — grammatically it is nothing but the plural you, and in most American contexts it lands as hostile
entries.type: personal pronoun (phrasal) — the appositive you + noun
entries.person / number: second person plural.
entries.refers to: the group being addressed — but, unlike you all or you guys, it addresses them as a category rather than as the people in the room. The noun does the damage: people invites the hearer to ask which people, and in the United States the answer supplied is usually race, ethnicity, religion, immigration status, class, or party. That reading is now the default one whatever the speaker intended, which is why the phrase turns up so often in coverage of public apologies. The neutral reading survives mainly when a modifier names a harmless category outright: you people in the back row, you people who ordered the fish.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms — you people are, you people were, you people have.
entries.pattern: You people [plural verb] · [verb] you people · [preposition] you people · you people who [verb] · you people in [place]
entries.contrast: Grammatically it is the same frame as you guys, you folks, you two, you editors — you plus a noun in apposition, taking the case of its slot, exactly like the us editors pattern under us. Pragmatically it is nothing like them. You all and y'all address a group as a group; you people addresses it as a type, and American listeners hear the type being named even when the speaker had none in mind. The most-cited instance is Ross Perot's 1992 address to the NAACP convention, where his repeated you people drew objections from the floor and took over the coverage. If the plural is all that is wanted, you all, all of you, folks, everyone, or the name of the group does the same work with none of the freight. Against your people, which is a different construction — possessive determiner plus noun — meaning the people belonging to or associated with you.
entries.see also: you, you all, you guys, y'all, youse, us, your (determiner)

entries.meaning: The Appalachian and western Pennsylvanian plural you, built from you ones. Locally it is an emblem of identity; outside its range it is unintelligible or heard as a joke.
examples: Yinz going down to the game on Sunday?
I'll save yinz a couple of seats.
Do you'uns need a ride back over the mountain?
Yinz guys want anything from the store?
Is that yinz' dog out in the yard?
entries.pronunciation note: two syllables, built like we'uns /ˈwiənz/; it also reduces to a one-syllable /junz/ (YOONZ), and the contracted Pittsburgh form yinz is /jɪnz/ (YINZ) — the same word one step further along
entries.русский: вы — диал. (Аппалачи, Питтсбург, где также yinz); вне литературной нормы
entries.register: nonstandard, strongly regionally marked
entries.type: personal pronoun, regional
entries.person / number: second person plural. From you ones, by way of Scots-Irish settlement.
