entries.refers to: the group being addressed. Geographically it is one of the tightest markers in American English: you'uns through Appalachia and the southern Midlands, yinz in and around Pittsburgh, where a native of the city is a Yinzer and the dialect itself is Yinzer or Pittsburghese.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms — yinz are, yinz were.
entries.pattern: Yinz [plural verb] · [verb] yinz · Yinz guys · yinz' [noun]
entries.contrast: Same job as y'all, you guys, and youse, different territory. You'uns and yinz are the most regionally restricted of the four and the most immediately identifying — using yinz outside western Pennsylvania reads as an imitation of Pittsburgh, not as a plural pronoun. Both are nonstandard in writing. The same dialects build a first person the same way: we'uns, with the object form us'uns.
entries.see also: you, y'all, you guys, youse, we'uns

entries.meaning: The northeastern urban plural you, built the obvious way: take you and add an -s. Recognize it; do not write it.
examples: Youse better hurry or you'll miss the train.
I told youse twice already.
What are youse guys doing out here?
This whole thing is on youse, not on me.
Are youse coming up for the holiday or not?
Are yous two coming, or should I hold the table?
Youse guys want anything from the deli?
entries.pronunciation note: also spelled yous
entries.русский: вы — прост., городское рабочее просторечие (Нью-Йорк, Филадельфия, Бостон)
entries.register: nonstandard, working-class urban
entries.type: personal pronoun, regional
entries.person / number: second person plural. Formed by adding the regular noun plural -s to you.
entries.refers to: the group being addressed. Associated with New York City, northern New Jersey, Philadelphia, Boston, and Chicago, and with Irish, Scottish, and Australian English — its American distribution tracks nineteenth-century Irish immigration closely.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms — youse are, youse were. The doubled youse guys is common and is treated as a single unit.
entries.pattern: Youse [plural verb] · [verb] youse · youse guys · youse guys' [noun]
entries.variants: yous (the commoner spelling in Philadelphia, and the usual one in Irish and Australian English), youse guys, yous guys — the doubled forms are one unit, plural twice over, and take a possessive as a unit (youse guys' car); youse and yous differ only in spelling
entries.contrast: Same function as y'all, you guys, and you'uns, different region and a heavier social marking than any of them — youse carries a working-class urban stereotype in the United States that y'all has largely shed. It is nonstandard everywhere in writing.
entries.see also: you, y'all, you guys, you'uns

entries.term: your Honor, Your Majesty, His Excellency
entries.meaning: A pronoun made out of a noun phrase, and the only place in modern English where a speaker addresses somebody in the third person on purpose. A learner meets it first in a courtroom, then in every costume drama ever filmed.
examples: Your Honor, the defense has no further questions for this witness.
If Your Honor is inclined to grant the continuance, we can be ready by the fourteenth.
May it please Your Honor, the exhibit was produced in discovery last spring.
His Excellency the Ambassador of Ireland will present his credentials on Tuesday.
Their Majesties were greeted at the airport by the governor and both senators.
Counsel rose and began, "Your Honor, may I approach the bench?"
The clerk read out the order, and Your Honor's signature was on the last page.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /jɚ ˈɑnɚ/ — y'r ON-er, which is what a courtroom actually sounds like. Your Majesty is /jɔr ˈmædʒəsti/ (yor-MAJ-uh-stee) and His Excellency is /hɪz ˈɛksələnsi/ (hiz-EK-suh-len-see), the h dropping when unstressed. Your Honour is the same word in British and Canadian spelling.
entries.русский: Ваша честь, Ваше Величество, Его Превосходительство — обращение по титулу вместо you
entries.case: subject and object alike; being a noun phrase, it fills any nominal slot
entries.register: formal, institutional, ceremonial
entries.type: honorific pronominal — a fixed noun phrase used in place of a pronoun
entries.person / number: third person singular in grammar, second person in reference — the strangest thing about these forms. Your Honor is spoken to the judge and takes the verb of a third person: Your Honor is correct, if Your Honor wishes. The Your- forms address the person; the His- and Her- forms speak about them. Plurals exist and take a plural verb: Their Majesties were received, Their Honors have ruled.
entries.refers to: the holder of an office, addressed by the office rather than by name or by you. In American practice Your Honor is the only one of the three an ordinary person is likely to say: it is the standard address to a judge in any American courtroom, and in some cities to a mayor. Your Majesty belongs to reigning monarchs and reaches Americans through British news, film, and history rather than through domestic life. His or Her Excellency is used of ambassadors and, in diplomatic correspondence, of heads of state and government, with Your Excellency as the vocative.
entries.agreement: third-person singular verb forms — Your Honor has the exhibit, His Excellency was received at noon. The possessive is formed on the noun, like any other noun phrase: Your Honor's ruling, His Excellency's residence.
entries.pattern: Your Honor, [clause] (vocative, set off by commas) · if Your Honor [third-person singular verb] · May it please the Court / May it please Your Honor · His Excellency [third-person singular verb] · Their Majesties [plural verb] · Your Honor's [noun]
entries.variants: Your Honour (British and Canadian spelling); Your Excellency as the vocative of His/Her Excellency; the parallel frames Your Holiness, Your Grace, Your Eminence, Mr. President, Madam Speaker, Mr. Chief Justice
entries.contrast: The your and his inside these phrases are possessive determiners, and as words they belong to the determiner dictionary — what acts as a pronoun here is the whole frozen phrase, exactly as with you guys and you all. Against plain you: both address the person in front of you, but the honorific converts the address into the third person, and that conversion is the grammar of deference — the same move as Would the gentleman yield? on the House floor. Capitalization is the written signal: Your Honor addressing the judge is capitalized, a judge of great honor is not. And the American set is narrower than the British one — My Lord, Your Worship, and Your Ladyship are not used in American courts, and in the U.S. Supreme Court advocates ordinarily say Justice Sotomayor and Mr. Chief Justice, with Your Honor also heard.
entries.see also: you, he, she, you all, you guys, your (determiner), his (determiner)

entries.meaning: One of the newer coinages, and one of the two — with fae / faer — that an American reader is likelier to meet in an online profile than anywhere in print.
examples: Ae joined the lab in September and has run the night shift ever since.
I sent aer the revised schedule on Tuesday and haven't heard back.
The badge reads "Wren Alcott (ae/aer), Facilities."
Ae is the only person on the crew who has read the manual all the way through.
Leave the packet with aer at the front desk.
Everything in the blue folder is aers; the red one is mine.
entries.pronunciation note: aer is /ɛr/ (AIR); a minority of users say /i/ (EE) for ae and /ˈeɪɚ/ (AY-er) for aer, and the person's own reading governs. Neither form has a schwa weak form; unstressed, they simply shorten, exactly as they does.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — гендерно-нейтральный набор ae/aer, с 2010-х
entries.case: ae subject, aer object and possessive determiner
entries.register: limited; one of the newer sets, in circulation in American online writing since the 2010s and met chiefly in profiles, signature lines, and rosters
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the ae / aer / aers / aerself set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ae (subject), aer (object), aer (determiner), aers (independent possessive), aerself (reflexive) — the same shape as fae / faer, with which it is easily confused.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ae / aer — human only, never a group, and never a hypothetical or generic person, which is singular they's job.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — ae is, ae was, ae has, ae does. Not ✗ae are: this is where the coined sets differ from singular they, which keeps the plural verb.
entries.pattern: Ae [singular verb] · [verb] aer · [preposition] aer · aer [noun] (the determiner use) · aers (standalone possessive) · aerself
entries.variants: cited ae/aer or ae/aer/aers; some listings give aers in the determiner slot as well
entries.contrast: Against fae / faer, built on exactly the same endings one letter over, and against ey and xe, which clip they/them rather than rhyming with it. The trap is homophony: aer is said like air and ae like the letter A, so Ae asked for the file reads for a beat as a typo — which is why writers who use the set gloss it once at first mention.
entries.see also: fae / faer, ey, ze, xe, they, possessive pronouns

entries.meaning: The nounself sets are the newest and rarest layer of this section, and bun is the one most often given as their example. They are not part of any traditional English paradigm and are not used by most speakers; where a person has stated one, it inflects across the same five slots as the older coined sets and takes the same singular verb.
examples: Bun has been running the server's art channel since it opened.
I asked bun to look over the draft before it went out to the group.
The bio line reads "Wren Alcott (bun/bunself), moderator."
Bun is the only one of us who remembered to bring a charger.
Leave the sketchbook with bun — bun asked for it back on Friday.
That's buns notebook on the table; don't move it. (the determiner use, which belongs with the determiners)
Bun built the whole site bunself over one weekend.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — one short syllable, and a perfect homophone of the ordinary noun bun. The possessive buns is /bʌnz/ (BUNZ) and the reflexive bunself is /bʌnˈsɛlf/ (bun-SELF), stressed on -self exactly as himself and themself are.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — nounself-набор от bunny «зайчик», интернет-среда
entries.case: subject and object alike, like you and it
entries.register: limited and rare; internet-native, met in online profiles, bios, and pronoun fields, and essentially never in speech, in print, or on workplace and campus forms
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — a nounself set, built out of the noun bunny rather than out of an existing pronoun
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The full paradigm runs bun (subject), bun (object), buns (possessive determiner), buns (independent possessive), bunself (reflexive) — five slots on the model of he / him / his / his / himself, with one form covering both cases and one covering both possessives.
entries.refers to: one specific person who has stated bun/bunself for themselves. Human only, never a group, and never a hypothetical or generic person — that is singular they's job, and it is the job no set in this section does. Nounself sets are introduced the way any other set is, and there is no way to infer one: a profile line, a bio, a signature, or an introduction (I'm Wren — bun/bunself).
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — bun is, bun was, bun has, bun does. Not ✗bun are: like every coined set here, and unlike singular they, it takes the singular verb.
entries.pattern: Bun [singular verb] · Bun [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] bun [verb]? · [verb] bun · [preposition] bun · buns [noun] (the determiner use) · buns (standalone possessive) · bunself
entries.variants: cited bun/bunself, bun/buns, or in full bun/bun/buns/bunself; some users write the set out as bunny/bunnyself, and the reflexive is occasionally bunnself
entries.contrast: Against fae / faer, the best-known nounself set and the only one shaped to look like a pronoun — fae rhymes with they, while bun does not disguise the noun it came from at all. Against star / starself and kit / kitself, the same construction on other nouns. Against the common noun bun, with which it is both homophone and homograph: Bun brought the folder stops a reader who does not know the set, which is why writers who use one name it once at first mention and then let it run. Before a noun buns is a determiner, not a pronoun — buns notebook belongs with the possessive determiners, and only the standalone use (the notebook is buns) is the pronoun.
entries.see also: star / starself, kit / kitself, fae / faer, ze, xe, they, reflexive and reciprocal pronouns

entries.meaning: The one coined pronoun in American English with a town's worth of native speakers rather than a scattering of individual ones.
examples: Co has been on the garden crew for three years.
I asked co to swap shifts with me on Thursday.
That's cos bicycle leaning against the dining hall. (the determiner use, which belongs with the determiners)
Co is teaching the beekeeping class this spring.
Nobody told co the meeting had moved to seven.
Co built the shelves coself, out of scrap from the woodshop.
entries.pronunciation note: no schwa weak form; unstressed it shortens without changing quality. Homophonous with the prefix co- and with the abbreviation Co., which is the one practical difficulty it has on the page.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — старейший из живых наборов, с 1970-х
entries.case: subject and object alike, like you and it
entries.register: limited; the oldest of the sets still in daily use, and the only one with a documented offline home
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the co / co / cos / coself set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. Invariant for case — Co called and I called co. The possessive cos covers both the determiner and the standalone slot; the reflexive is coself.
entries.refers to: one specific person. Co was coined by Mary Orovan in 1970 and has been in continuous use since the 1970s at Twin Oaks Community, an intentional community in Louisa County, Virginia, whose bylaws and everyday speech use it as the ordinary third-person pronoun for everybody — which makes it the rare neopronoun an American might hear spoken all day in one place rather than read in a profile.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — co is, co was, co has, co does.
entries.pattern: Co [singular verb] · [verb] co · [preposition] co · cos [noun] · coself
entries.variants: the possessive is also written co's; the set is cited co/cos
entries.contrast: Against per, the other case-invariant set of the 1970s — neither marks subject against object, so both behave like you rather than like he/him. Against it, which is also invariant across cases but carries a history co does not. In print the difficulty is the abbreviation: Co opening a sentence can read as a truncated company name, which is why documents that use it often set it in italics the first time. Before a noun cos is a determiner, not a pronoun — cos bicycle belongs with the possessive determiners; only the standalone use (the bicycle is cos) is the pronoun.
entries.see also: per, it (as a chosen personal pronoun), ze, they, pers

entries.meaning: The object form of the Spivak set — the family built by subtraction rather than invention. Michael Spivak used E / Em / Eir in his TeX manual in the 1980s and gave the set its usual name; the early-1990s text world LambdaMOO offered "Spivak" as a gender setting, which is where a great many American internet users first met it.
examples: I sent em the draft on Friday and got notes back the same night.
Ask em whether the lab still needs a second reader.
The package on the porch is for em, not for the downstairs apartment.
We hired em out of the Denver office in 2019.
Give the extra ticket to Priya and em.
Said aloud, tell em and tell 'em are the same sentence; only the writing says whether one person or a crowd is meant.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /əm/ — and in that weak form it is a homophone of 'em, the reduced them. The resemblance is not an accident: the set is they / them / their with the th- clipped off the front.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — объектная форма набора ey/em (местоимения Спивака)
entries.register: limited; in circulation since the mid-1970s, and met by Americans in online writing, in some science fiction and academic prose, and in pronoun introductions
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the object form of the ey / em / eir set, usually called the Spivak pronouns
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ey (subject), em (object), eir (determiner), eirs (independent possessive), emself (reflexive).
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ey / em — human only, never a group.
entries.agreement: none of its own — an object controls no verb. The subject form takes a singular verb (ey is), where singular they takes are.
entries.pattern: [verb] em · [verb] em [direct object] · [preposition] em · eir [noun] · eirs (standalone possessive) · emself
entries.variants: capitalized Em in Michael Spivak's original E / Em / Eir; the lowercase ey / em / eir is Christine Elverson's 1975 revision, which won a contest for a gender-neutral pronoun and is the form in general use; the reflexive is written emself and, less often, eirself
entries.contrast: Against 'em — one sound, two unrelated words. 'em is the thirteen-hundred-year-old survival of Old English heom, unstressed and available to every English speaker; em is a deliberate coinage of the 1970s and 1980s, used of one specific person. Speech does not distinguish them at all, and the apostrophe does all the work on the page. Against them: em is what is left of them once the th- comes off, which is also why emself looks the way it does.
entries.see also: ey, 'em, them, eirs, they

entries.meaning: The subject form of the Spivak pronouns, and the most-used of the coinages built by clipping an existing word rather than inventing a new one.
examples: Ey runs the reading room on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
Did ey say when the transcript would be ready?
Ey has been with the firm longer than anyone else on this floor.
My co-author and ey presented the paper together in Boston.
Ey wrote the whole grant application emself in four days.
When ey is on call, the schedule shows "L. Ahmadi (ey/em)."
entries.pronunciation note: no schwa weak form; the diphthong shortens when unstressed, exactly as in they, from which the form was made by dropping the th-.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — подлежащная форма набора ey/em, местоимения Спивака
entries.register: limited; in circulation since the mid-1970s, commoner in online and academic writing than in speech
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the subject form of the ey / em / eir set, the Spivak pronouns
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ey (subject), em (object), eir (determiner), eirs (independent possessive), emself (reflexive).
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ey / em — human only, never a group, and not a generic epicene.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — ey is, ey was, ey has, ey does. This is where the Spivak set parts company with the they it was clipped from: they keeps the plural verb even for one person, ey takes the singular. Some users say ey are by analogy; the person's own practice settles it.
entries.pattern: Ey [singular verb] · Ey [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] ey [verb]? · eir [noun] · emself
entries.variants: capitalized E (Michael Spivak's spelling); lowercase ey (Christine Elverson's 1975 revision, and the usual modern form)
entries.contrast: Against they: same origin, different agreement — the whole point of the set was a singular pronoun that looks singular and takes a singular verb. Against ae, which sounds like the letter A and belongs to a different set entirely. In running speech ey is close enough to the interjection eh that writers name the set once at first mention and then let it run.
entries.see also: em (Spivak object), they, eirs, ze, xe

entries.meaning: The best-known of the nounself sets, and a form a learner is far likelier to meet online than at work.
examples: Fae has been moderating the forum since it opened.
I told faer the meeting had moved to Thursday.
That's faers — the green notebook with the sticker on the cover.
Fae is bringing the extra chairs, so we don't have to rent any.
Ask faer to send the photos when fae gets home.
The roster shows "Ari Delacroix (fae/faer)" in the pronoun column.
entries.pronunciation note: faer is /fɛr/ (FAIR); neither has a weak form, and both simply shorten when unstressed.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — nounself-набор от fae «фея»
entries.case: fae subject, faer object and possessive determiner
entries.register: limited; an internet-era coinage in circulation since the 2010s, met in profiles, fan communities, and rosters rather than in print
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the fae / faer / faers / faerself set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs fae (subject), faer (object), faer (determiner), faers (independent possessive), faerself (reflexive).
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses fae / faer — human only. The form is built from the noun fae, a fairy, in the older spelling fay, which puts it in the group sometimes called nounself pronouns: sets built out of an ordinary noun rather than out of an existing pronoun. That origin is why it is likelier to be met in an online community than in a workplace directory.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — fae is, fae was, fae has.
entries.pattern: Fae [singular verb] · [verb] faer · [preposition] faer · faer [noun] · faers (standalone possessive) · faerself
entries.variants: cited fae/faer or fae/faer/faers; the spellings fey and feyr are occasionally used for the same set
entries.contrast: Against ae / aer, built on identical endings — a letter apart in writing, clearly distinct in speech. Against the common noun fae, which is what a reader who does not know the set will take it for. Against ze and xe, which are older, commoner, and built as pronouns from the start rather than out of a noun.
entries.see also: ae / aer, ze, xe, they, possessive pronouns

entries.meaning: The object form of the first neopronoun set to reach a wide American readership, and still the one most often met in writing from the 1990s and 2000s.
examples: I called hir twice from the airport and got voicemail both times.
The committee offered hir the position on Friday afternoon.
This envelope is for hir, not for me.
Nobody had told hir that the deadline moved.
Give the spare key to Dana and hir before you leave.
Ze wrote the report hirself, over one weekend.
entries.pronunciation note: also /hɚ/ (HUR) for a minority of users, which makes it a perfect homophone of her; most say /hɪr/ precisely to keep the two apart. Weak /(h)ɪr/ — the /h/ drops when the word is unstressed and non-initial, exactly as it does in him and her: tell hir [ˈtɛl ɪr].
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — объектная и притяжательная форма набора ze/hir
entries.case: object, and also the possessive determiner (hir coat)
entries.register: limited; the object form of the 1990s wave of coinages, met in writing from that period, in trans and genderqueer communities, and wherever a person states it
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the object form of the ze / hir and sie / hir sets
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ze, zie, or sie (subject), hir (object and determiner), hirs (independent possessive), hirself (reflexive).
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ze / hir — human only, never a group. The pairing was current in American trans and genderqueer writing and on the early internet in the 1990s; the writer Leslie Feinberg used ze and hir in print in that decade, which is where many readers first met the set.
entries.agreement: none of its own — an object controls no verb. The subject form takes a singular verb (ze is).
entries.pattern: [verb] hir · [verb] hir [direct object] · [preposition] hir · hir [noun] (the determiner use) · hirs (standalone possessive) · hirself
entries.variants: hir also fills the independent possessive slot for some users (the coat is hir), on the model of his, though hirs is the regularized form; the subject form is written ze, zie, and sie
entries.contrast: Against zir: the same slot in a different pairing — ze/hir is the older set, ze/zir the one that regularized everything around z-, and which of the two a person uses is a fact about the person, not about the words. Against her: one letter apart on paper, and for speakers who say /hɪr/ clearly distinct in speech; for the minority who say /hɚ/ the two are homophones and only the writing separates them. Before a noun hir is a determiner, not a pronoun — hir coat belongs with the possessive determiners, and the standalone possessive is hirs.
entries.see also: ze, zir, hirs, her, them, themself

entries.meaning: One of the two-hundred-odd gender-neutral third-person pronouns proposed in English since the 1780s, and one of the handful still carried in current listings. It is not part of any traditional paradigm and is not used by most speakers; where it is used, it is used for one person who has stated it, and it inflects across all five slots like every other set in this section.
examples: Hu has taught the Thursday seminar for four years running.
Did hu say whether the transcript would be ready before the hearing?
I left the packet with hum at the front desk.
Hu is the only person on the committee who read the appendix.
That's hus bicycle chained to the rail outside. (the determiner use, which belongs with the determiners)
The green folder is hus; the blue one is mine.
Hu wrote the entire proposal humself in a week.
entries.pronunciation note: homophonous with hue and with the name Hugh. Hum is /hjum/ (HYOOM) and hus /hjuz/ (HYOOZ) for users who keep the vowel of human, the word the set is clipped from; others read the spellings by ordinary English rules and say /hʌm/ (HUM) and /hʌs/ (HUSS). All three drop the /h/ when unstressed and non-initial, exactly as him, her, and his do — tell hum [ˈtɛl (j)əm] — which puts the object form within a hair of 'em at conversational speed.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — набор hu/hum, усечение от human (1982), редк.
entries.case: hu subject, hum object, hus possessive determiner and independent possessive alike
entries.register: limited and rare; a proposal of the early 1980s that stayed in the pronoun listings without ever reaching general use, met today in those listings, in profiles, and occasionally in fiction rather than in print or in speech
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the hu / hum / hus / humself set, clipped from human
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs hu (subject), hum (object), hus (determiner and independent possessive), humself (reflexive) — four distinct forms across five slots, the possessive doing double duty the way his does.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses hu / hum — human only, which is the whole point of a form clipped from human, and never a group or a generic person. The set is usually credited to Sasha Newborn, who published it in Santa Barbara in 1982, and it belongs to the long American line of gender-neutral coinages Dennis Baron catalogues in What's Your Pronoun? — more than two hundred since the 1780s, almost none of which entered the general language.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms for the subject — hu is, hu was, hu has, hu does, not ✗hu are. Hum and hus, being an object and a possessive, control no verb at all.
entries.pattern: Hu [singular verb] · Hu [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] hu [verb]? · [verb] hum · [preposition] hum · hus [noun] (the determiner use) · hus (standalone possessive) · humself
entries.variants: cited hu/hum, hu/hus, or in full hu/hum/hus/humself; the reflexive is written humself and, less often, huself; a reduced paradigm appears in some listings with hu covering subject and object alike
entries.contrast: Against per and co, the other sets pulled out of an ordinary word rather than invented from nothing — per from person, hu from human — and, like them, far rarer in American pronoun listings than ze or xe. Against him and his, which hum and hus sit one letter away from and collapse into once the /h/ goes: unstressed, hum and him are both [əm], and only the writing separates them. Against 'em for the same reason. Before a noun hus is a determiner, not a pronoun — hus coat belongs with the possessive determiners; only the standalone use (the coat is hus) is the pronoun.
entries.see also: per, co, ze, xe, they, 'em, him, reflexive and reciprocal pronouns

entries.meaning: The one pronoun in this section that was already in the dictionary. Everything about it is ordinary except who is entitled to apply it.
examples: The directory entry reads "Robin Ash (it/its), staff photographer."
Robin asked the team to use it, so that is what the team uses.
It had already read the whole packet before the meeting started.
I left the revised print with it at the front desk.
The blue camera bag by the door is its.
Some people use two sets, and the roster shows it/they — either one is right.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ət/ — identical in every respect to the ordinary it; nothing in the sound distinguishes the two uses.
entries.русский: оно — обычное it как выбранное самим человеком местоимение; иначе звучит как оскорбление
entries.register: limited, and conditional on consent — neutral when it is the pronoun a person has stated, an insult when it is not
entries.type: personal pronoun, in its chosen personal use
entries.person / number: third person singular. The paradigm is the ordinary one: it (subject and object), its (determiner and independent possessive), itself (reflexive).
entries.refers to: one specific person who has stated it/its for themselves. A small number of people — mostly young, mostly nonbinary — use it/its, sometimes alone and sometimes paired with another set (it/they, it/she). This is the one item in this section that is not a coinage at all: it is the existing English it, applied to a person by that person's own choice.
entries.agreement: third-person singular verb forms — it is, it was, it has, exactly as with the ordinary it.
entries.pattern: It [singular verb] · [verb] it · [preposition] it · its [noun] · itself · the roster form it/its
entries.variants: listed as it/its, and often paired — it/they, it/she, it/he — where a person uses more than one set
entries.contrast: Against the ordinary it, from which it differs in nothing grammatical: same forms, same agreement, same slots. The entire difference is the referent and the permission. English's ordinary rule is that it cannot refer to a human being, and the reason that rule matters is that calling a person it has been a standard way of denying that they are one; that history is exactly why the chosen use turns on the person having asked for it, and why it does not generalize to anyone else. Against they, which is what an American writer uses when a person's pronoun is unknown.
entries.see also: it, they, itself, its (determiner), ze

entries.meaning: A nounself set built on kit, the word for a young fox or rabbit. Like the rest of that family it is not part of any traditional English paradigm and is not used by most speakers; it inflects across the same five slots as the older coined sets, takes a singular verb, and belongs to whoever has stated it.
examples: Kit joined the forum two years ago and has moderated it ever since.
I sent kit the revised map on Sunday night and got notes back by morning.
Everything in the shared folder came from kit.
Kit is the only person here who can still read the old file format.
Hold the door for kit — kit is carrying both boxes.
That's kits headset on the desk; leave it where it is. (the determiner use)
Kit finished the translation kitself, without a dictionary.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; a single short syllable and a perfect homophone of the ordinary noun kit. The possessive kits is /kɪts/ (KITS) — indistinguishable in speech from the plural kits and from the noun's own possessive kit's — and the reflexive kitself is /kɪtˈsɛlf/ (kit-SELF), stressed on -self like itself and himself.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — nounself-набор от kit «лисёнок, крольчонок»
entries.register: limited and rare; internet-native, met in online profiles and pronoun fields rather than in speech, in print, or on institutional forms
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — a nounself set, built out of the noun kit, a young fox, rabbit, or ferret
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs kit (subject), kit (object), kits (possessive determiner), kits (independent possessive), kitself (reflexive).
entries.refers to: one specific person who has stated kit/kitself. Human only, never a group, and never a generic or hypothetical person — singular they covers that and no coined set does. Like the other nounself sets it is stated rather than inferred, and it is stated in the ordinary places: a profile field, a bio line, an introduction.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — kit is, kit was, kit has, kit does, not ✗kit are.
entries.pattern: Kit [singular verb] · Kit [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] kit [verb]? · [verb] kit · [preposition] kit · kits [noun] (the determiner use) · kits (standalone possessive) · kitself
entries.variants: cited kit/kitself or kit/kits; the possessive is also written kit's, which buys back the distinction from the plural noun at the cost of colliding with the noun's own possessive
entries.contrast: Against bun / bunself and star / starself, the same construction on different nouns. Against the common noun kit — a toolkit, a drum kit, a model kit — which is the commoner word by an enormous margin, so Kit is ready is a sentence about a person only for a reader who already knows the set. Against the given name Kit, short for Christopher or Katherine, which is the other thing a reader assumes first. That double collision is the practical argument for naming the set at first mention wherever it appears in running prose. Before a noun kits is a determiner, not a pronoun — kits headset belongs with the possessive determiners.
entries.see also: bun / bunself, star / starself, fae / faer, it (as a chosen personal pronoun), ze, they

entries.meaning: A set built on the they/them frame, and a reminder that the same idea has been tried more than once: a ne turns up among the nineteenth-century proposals as well as in the current listings.
examples: Ne teaches the Tuesday section and grades the Thursday one.
I passed nem in the hallway and forgot to ask about the schedule.
Nir office is the one at the end with the plant in the window. (the determiner use, which belongs with the determiners)
We asked nem to look at the numbers before the board meeting.
Ne has been rewriting the intake form nemself since March.
The sign-up sheet lists "Sasha Voight (ne/nem)" for the morning shift.
entries.pronunciation note: nem is /nɛm/ (NEM), weak /nəm/ — the same reduction them takes, and for the same reason: the set is modeled on they / them.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — набор ne/nem/nir, редк.
entries.register: limited and rare; met in online pronoun listings and profiles rather than in print
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the ne / nem / nir / nirs / nemself set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ne (subject), nem (object), nir (determiner), nirs (independent possessive), nemself (reflexive).
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ne / nem — human only, never a group.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms for the subject — ne is, ne was, ne has. Nem, being an object, controls no verb.
entries.pattern: Ne [singular verb] · [verb] nem · [preposition] nem · nir [noun] · nirs (standalone possessive) · nemself
entries.variants: cited ne/nem or ne/nem/nir; a nineteenth-century ne / nis / nim appears among the older proposals and shares only the subject form
entries.contrast: Against ey and em (Spivak object), built the same way — take they / them / their and replace the th- — and much commoner. Against em: nem and em are one consonant apart and belong to two different sets, which is the practical argument for naming a set at first mention. Before a noun nir is a determiner, not a pronoun — nir office belongs with the possessive determiners; only the standalone nirs is the pronoun.
entries.see also: ey, em (Spivak object), they, xe, ze

entries.meaning: The one coinage that came into English through a novel, and the one whose homophone problem is with a preposition rather than with another pronoun.
examples: Per took the early train and got in ahead of the storm.
I gave per the keys to the shop on Friday.
That's pers jacket on the back of the chair. (the determiner use, which belongs with the determiners)
Per is the one who noticed the error in the totals.
Nobody had told per that the route changed.
In Piercy's novel everyone in the village is per, and the word stops being strange after a page.
entries.pronunciation note: no separate weak form. Homophonous with the preposition per (per diem, miles per hour) and with purr, which is the one real difficulty the form has.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — набор per, усечение от person (М. Пирси, 1976)
entries.case: subject and object alike, like you and it
entries.register: limited and rare; an American meets it chiefly in feminist science fiction, and occasionally where a person states it
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the per / per / pers / perself set, clipped from person
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. One form covers subject, object, and — for many users — the determiner; the independent possessive is pers and the reflexive perself.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses per — human only, which is the point of a form clipped from person. The set entered general circulation through Marge Piercy's 1976 novel Woman on the Edge of Time, where it is the ordinary pronoun of the future the book imagines, and that novel is where most American readers have met it.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — per is, per was, per has, per does.
entries.pattern: Per [singular verb] · [verb] per · [preposition] per · pers [noun] · perself
entries.variants: per also fills the possessive determiner slot in many listings (per coat), in which case the set is given as per / per / per / perself; pers is the regularized independent possessive
entries.contrast: Against co, the other case-invariant set of the 1970s — neither marks subject against object, so both work like you rather than like he/him. Against the Latin preposition per, a different word entirely that is never a pronoun, though it does make per coat readable two ways for a beat. Against ze and xe, which mark case and are far commoner in American pronoun listings. Before a noun per or pers is a determiner, not a pronoun — pers jacket belongs with the possessive determiners; only the standalone use (the jacket is pers) is the pronoun.
entries.see also: co, pers, ve, they, it

entries.meaning: A nounself set built on star. It is not part of any traditional English paradigm and is not used by most speakers; where a person has stated it, it inflects across the same five slots as the older coined sets and takes a singular verb, and it is introduced the same way every set in this section is — on a badge, in a bio, or in a sentence of introduction.
examples: Star has been running the Thursday reading group since last winter.
I asked star to send the photos over when star got home.
The introduction went, "This is Rowan — star/starself, if you're taking notes."
Star is bringing the projector, so nobody has to rent one.
Leave the packet with star at the front desk.
Everything on the second shelf is stars.
Star wrote the grant application starself over two weekends.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form. The possessive stars is /stɑrz/ (STARZ), homophonous with the plural noun stars and with the noun's possessive star's; the reflexive starself is /stɑrˈsɛlf/ (star-SELF), stressed on -self.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — nounself-набор от star «звезда»
entries.register: limited and rare; internet-native, met in profiles, bios, and pronoun fields rather than in speech or in print
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — a nounself set, built out of the ordinary noun star
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs star (subject), star (object), stars (possessive determiner), stars (independent possessive), starself (reflexive).
entries.refers to: one specific person who has stated star/starself. Human only, never a group, and never a generic or hypothetical person. As with the other nounself sets, the noun the form is built from is part of why a person chose it, and the set is announced rather than deduced.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — star is, star was, star has, star does, not ✗star are.
entries.pattern: Star [singular verb] · Star [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] star [verb]? · [verb] star · [preposition] star · stars [noun] (the determiner use) · stars (standalone possessive) · starself
entries.variants: cited star/starself or star/stars; the possessive is also written star's
entries.contrast: Against bun / bunself and kit / kitself, built the same way on other nouns, and against fae / faer, the nounself set old enough and common enough to have its own following. Against the ordinary noun star, which carries two everyday senses at once — the object in the sky and the celebrity — so Star was late is readable three ways until context settles it. The possessive is the harder collision: spoken stars is the plural noun, the noun's possessive, and the pronoun's determiner all at the same time, which is why writers using the set often spell it star's to buy one distinction back. Before a noun stars is a determiner, not a pronoun — stars notes belongs with the possessive determiners.
entries.see also: bun / bunself, kit / kitself, fae / faer, ze, xe, they

entries.meaning: The convention that lets a whole paradigm be named in a badge-sized space. It is a piece of American workplace and campus orthography rather than a word of the language, and it is the form in which most Americans first meet any pronoun set they did not grow up with.
examples: The signature line reads "Dana Whitlock (they/them), Director of Admissions."
"Hi, I'm Marcus, he/him — I'll be running the workshop this morning."
The registration form takes any set: she/her, he/him, they/them, ze/hir, or free text.
Her card says she/her, his says he/him, and the new analyst's says ze/zir.
Some people list two sets — she/they means either one is fine.
The form used to say "preferred pronouns" and now says just "pronouns."
entries.pronunciation note: the slash is never read aloud — she/her is said she her, ze/hir is said zee heer, and a three-part label (xe/xem/xyr) is read the same way. In writing, the slash is the whole convention.
entries.русский: «она/её», «они/их» — не местоимение, а запись через слэш названия набора форм
entries.case: none; the label is a noun phrase (my pronouns are they/them)
entries.register: neutral; standard in email signatures, name badges, class rosters, staff directories, conference programs, and spoken introductions
entries.type: citation label — a pronoun set named by two or three of its forms, used as the set's name rather than as a pronoun
entries.person / number: not applicable — the label names a paradigm rather than pointing at anybody. The person it belongs to is named separately, right beside it.
entries.refers to: the whole set of forms a person uses. She/her stands for she, her, hers, herself; they/them for they, them, their, theirs, themself; ze/hir for ze, hir, hirs, hirself. Two forms — subject and object — are the American norm, and a third is added where the possessive is not predictable from the first two (ze/hir/hirs, xe/xem/xyr). A slash between two whole sets (she/they, it/they) means the person uses both.
entries.agreement: the label behaves as a fixed name, and the verb follows the sentence rather than the pronoun inside the label: My pronouns are they/them, "She/her" is what the badge says.
entries.pattern: my pronouns are [set] · [name] (they/them) · Pronouns: she/her · goes by [set] · [set] / [set] (two sets, either acceptable) · I'm Marcus, he/him
entries.variants: two-form labels (he/him), three-form labels (xe/xem/xyr), paired sets (she/they), and the older preferred pronouns, now generally shortened to pronouns
entries.contrast: The label is not the pronoun. She/her in a signature block names a paradigm; she in a sentence does a pronoun's work, and putting the label where a pronoun belongs is a category error — ✗I asked she/her to send the file is I asked her to send the file. American institutional style has largely dropped preferred pronouns for plain pronouns, on the reasoning that a pronoun is not a preference. And a label naming two sets is an invitation rather than a puzzle: either one is correct.
entries.see also: they, she, he, ze, hir, xe, it (as a chosen personal pronoun), themself

entries.meaning: The subject form of the set that science fiction carried further than the internet did.
examples: Ve wrote the simulation code and the paper that came out of it.
Did ve say whether the run finished overnight?
Ve has been at the institute since the first grant cycle.
My co-author and ve are presenting on the same panel.
Ve is the only person here who reads the release notes.
In Egan's novels ve is ordinary, which is what a whole book of it does to a reader's ear.
entries.pronunciation note: no schwa weak form; it shortens when unstressed, like we, with which it rhymes and is occasionally confused by ear.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — подлежащная форма набора ve/ver (науч. фантастика)
entries.register: limited and rare; met mainly in science fiction — Greg Egan's novels are where most American readers have run into it — and in online pronoun listings
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the subject form of the ve / ver set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ve (subject), ver (object), vis or ver (determiner), vers or vis (independent possessive), verself (reflexive).
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ve / ver — human only, never a group.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — ve is, ve was, ve has, ve does.
entries.pattern: Ve [singular verb] · Ve [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] ve [verb]? · vis [noun] · verself
entries.variants: two paradigms compete — ve / ver / vis / vis / verself, the shape Greg Egan's fiction uses, and ve / ver / vers / vers / verself, built with the regular -s; a reader who has met one will not necessarily recognize the other
entries.contrast: Against ver, its own object form. Against we, which it rhymes with — the reason writers using the set name it once at first mention. Against ze and xe, which are commoner in American pronoun listings by a wide margin.
entries.see also: ver, vers, per, they, we

entries.meaning: The object form of the ve set, and the neopronoun most easily mistaken for an ordinary word of English.
examples: I emailed ver the revised figures on Sunday night.
The reviewers sent ver three pages of comments.
Sit next to ver — there's room at that end of the table.
We hired ver out of the Melbourne office two years ago.
Everything in the shared folder came from ver.
Hand the badge to ver at the door; ve is expecting it.
entries.pronunciation note: rhymes with her and fur; already reduced in shape, and it has no further weak form.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — объектная форма набора ve/ver
entries.case: object, and also the possessive determiner in the paradigm that does not use vis
entries.register: limited and rare, on the same terms as ve
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the object form of the ve / ver set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ve / ver — human only, never a group.
entries.agreement: none of its own — an object controls no verb. The subject form takes a singular verb (ve is).
entries.pattern: [verb] ver · [verb] ver [direct object] · [preposition] ver · ver [noun] (in the paradigm without vis) · vers (standalone possessive) · verself
entries.variants: vis is the possessive determiner in Greg Egan's paradigm (vis notes) and ver in the other; the independent possessive is vers or vis to match
entries.contrast: Against her, which it rhymes with exactly — a listener who does not know the set hears the wrong pronoun rather than an unfamiliar one, which is the strongest argument for naming the set at first mention. Against vis, which precedes a noun and is therefore a determiner, dictionaried with the possessive determiners. Against xem and zir, the object forms of the two commoner sets.
entries.see also: ve, vers, zir, xem, them

entries.meaning: The commonest of the x- sets, and the one American campus and workplace forms list most often after she/her, he/him, and they/them.
examples: Xe joined the department last fall and teaches two sections of the survey.
Did xe get the revised syllabus in time?
Xe has been running the outreach program since it started.
My advisor and xe wrote the proposal together.
Xe is the only one of us who can still read the old code.
The roster line reads "J. Okonkwo (xe/xem)."
entries.pronunciation note: the x- spells /z/, so the word begins like zebra, not like ex; a minority say /ksi/ (KSEE). For most speakers xe and ze are homophones, and only the spelling tells the two sets apart. No schwa weak form.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — подлежащная форма набора xe/xem/xyr
entries.register: limited; in American online writing since the 1990s, and one of the more frequently listed sets today alongside ze / zir and ey / em
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the subject form of the xe / xem / xyr set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs xe (subject), xem (object), xyr (determiner, also written xir), xyrs (independent possessive), xemself (reflexive).
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses xe / xem — human only, never a group, and not a generic epicene.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — xe is, xe was, xe has, xe does, where singular they takes the plural verb.
entries.pattern: Xe [singular verb] · Xe [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] xe [verb]? · xyr [noun] · xemself
entries.variants: xe / xem / xir; the same set is also written ze / zem / zyr; cited xe/xem or xe/xem/xyr
entries.contrast: Against ze: identical in speech for most users, different in writing, and the sets are not interchangeable — a person who writes xe/xem/xyr is not using ze/hir. Against singular they, which is the standard form and takes a plural verb. The spelling is the practical difficulty: a reader meeting xe cold tries /ks/ or /ɛks/ first, which is why writers who use it gloss the pronunciation once.
entries.see also: xem, xyrs, ze, zir, they

entries.meaning: The object form of the xe set, built by putting an x where the th of them used to be.
examples: I sent xem the contract on Tuesday.
Ask xem whether the room is booked for Thursday.
The award went to xem and to the two graduate students.
We ran into xem at the conference in Baltimore.
Hold the elevator for xem — xe is right behind me.
Everything on the second shelf belongs to xem.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /zəm/ — the reduction them takes, which is where the shape comes from. The x- spells /z/.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — объектная форма набора xe/xem
entries.register: limited; the object form of one of the more frequently listed American neopronoun sets
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the object form of the xe / xem / xyr set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses xe / xem — human only, never a group.
entries.agreement: none of its own — an object controls no verb. The subject form takes a singular verb (xe is).
entries.pattern: [verb] xem · [verb] xem [direct object] · [preposition] xem · xyr [noun] · xyrs (standalone possessive) · xemself
entries.variants: the reflexive is xemself and, less often, xyrself; the spelling zem belongs to the same set
entries.contrast: Against zir and hir, the object forms of the other two common sets — three different words for one slot, and which one is right is a fact about the person rather than about English. Against them, from which xem takes both its shape and its weak form. Against 'em: in fast speech tell xem and tell 'em differ only by the /z/ at the front, so this is a form that benefits from being written down.
entries.see also: xe, xyrs, zir, hir, them

entries.meaning: The most-used of the coined sets, and the one an American is likeliest to meet on a badge or in a signature line.
examples: Ze has run the community garden for six years.
Did ze say when the grant report is due?
Ze is teaching the Wednesday workshop this term.
My neighbor and ze built the whole fence over one weekend.
Ze hasn't answered an email since the conference.
The directory lists "Sam Reyes (ze/hir), Program Coordinator."
entries.pronunciation note: also /zeɪ/ (ZAY) for a minority of users. The variant spellings zie /zi/ and sie /si/ belong to the same set. No schwa weak form; like she it simply shortens when unstressed. For most speakers ze and xe are homophones.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — самый частый; подлежащная форма ze/hir и ze/zir
entries.register: limited; the most widely used of the American neopronouns, met in pronoun introductions, email signatures, name badges, class rosters, and profiles
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the subject form of the ze / hir and ze / zir sets
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. Two paradigms share this subject form: ze / hir / hirs / hirself, the older pairing, and ze / zir / zirs / zirself, which regularized everything around z-.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ze — human only, never a group, and never a hypothetical or generic person, which is singular they's job. The set emerged in American trans and genderqueer writing and on the early internet in the 1990s; the writer Leslie Feinberg used ze and hir in print in that decade.
entries.agreement: singular verb forms — ze is, ze was, ze has, ze does. Singular they keeps its plural verb; ze does not.
entries.pattern: Ze [singular verb] · Ze [auxiliary] [verb] · [auxiliary] ze [verb]? · hir or zir [noun] · hirself or zirself
entries.variants: zie, sie; the object form is hir for some users and zir for others, and the pairing is a fact about the person rather than about the word
entries.contrast: Against xe: the same sound, a different spelling tradition, and a different set — ze/hir and xe/xem/xyr are not interchangeable in writing. Against singular they, which is standard, far commoner, and takes a plural verb. Against hir and zir, the two object forms this subject form pairs with; the entry for each says which set it belongs to.
entries.see also: hir, zir, hirs, zirs, xe, they

entries.meaning: The object form of the regularized z- set, and the neopronoun most often paired with ze on American forms today. ---
examples: I emailed zir the schedule on Monday.
Ask zir whether the studio is free on Saturday.
The package on the counter is for zir.
We met zir at the conference in Portland two years ago.
Give the extra badge to Priya and zir.
That's zir jacket on the hook by the door. (the determiner use, which belongs with the determiners)
entries.pronunciation note: also /zɚ/ (ZUR); weak /zɚ/. The variant spelling xir is pronounced the same way and belongs with the xe spelling of the set.
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — объектная и притяжательная форма набора ze/zir
entries.case: object, and also the possessive determiner (zir coat)
entries.register: limited; one of the more frequently used American neopronoun forms, met in signatures, badges, rosters, and profiles
entries.type: personal pronoun; neopronoun — the object form of the ze / zir set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ze or zie (subject), zir (object and determiner), zirs (independent possessive), zirself (reflexive).
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ze / zir — human only, never a group.
entries.agreement: none of its own — an object controls no verb. The subject form takes a singular verb (ze is).
entries.pattern: [verb] zir · [verb] zir [direct object] · [preposition] zir · zir [noun] (the determiner use) · zirs (standalone possessive) · zirself
entries.variants: xir, the spelling used alongside xe, and zer; zir also fills the independent possessive slot for some users, on the model of his, though zirs is the regularized form
entries.contrast: Against hir: the same slot in the older pairing, and the choice between them belongs to the person, not to the grammar. Against xem, the object form of the xe set. Against sir, with which it rhymes for speakers who say /zɚ/ — a real source of mishearing on the telephone. Before a noun zir is a determiner, not a pronoun — zir coat belongs with the possessive determiners, and the standalone possessive is zirs.
entries.see also: ze, hir, zirs, xem, xe, they
